en: [The Chapter on Conduct] [1. The Introductory Section] Having honored Yājñavalkya, the Lord of Yogins, the sages spoke:
Tell us, without omission, the duties of those belonging to the castes, the stages of life, and others.
Remaining in Mithilā, that lord of yogis meditated for a moment and said to the sages:
"Learn the duties in that country where the black antelope roams. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.2)
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) of the Vedas—these fourteen are the repositories of knowledge and of dharma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.3)
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.4)
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
Whatever substance, accompanied by faith, is given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time through the appropriate means— that is entirely the characteristic of dharma.
Revelation, tradition, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.7)
Of the acts of sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the study of scripture, this indeed is the supreme duty: the perception of the Self through yoga.

An assembly consisting of four who know the Vedas and the Dharma, or even those who possess the threefold knowledge (traividya), shall declare that which is the Dharma; or else, a single person who is most excellent among those who know the inner self (adhyātma).
[2. The Section on the Religious Student (Brahmacārin)] The castes are the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, indeed, the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral ground are performed with sacred formulas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.10)

The rite of conception (garbhādhāna) should be performed during the fertile period; the rite for ensuring a male child (pumsavana) before the fetus moves; the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) in the sixth or eighth month; and these [rites], along with the birth ceremony (jātakarman), are to be performed within one month [of birth]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.11)
On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month the going-forth;
in the sixth month the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be performed according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb is pacified;
these rites for women are performed silently, but their marriage is accompanied by mantras.

The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year after conception or in the eighth year [itself]; for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh year plus one; and for Vaiśyas, in the twelfth year, or according to family custom.
Having initiated the pupil with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) as a preliminary,
the teacher should teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purification and conduct.
During the day and at the twilights, one should void urine and feces facing north with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) over the ear; if it is at night, one should face south.
Having risen with his penis still held, he should, with alertness, perform purification using earth and drawn-up water so as to remove both odor and residue. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.17)
Seated with his knees together in a clean place, facing either north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand, are respectively the *prājāpatya*, *pitrya*, *brāhma*, and *daiva* tīrthas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.19)
Having sipped water three times and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch the cavities of the head with water—
water that is natural, free from foam and bubbles.
The twice-born classes are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively;
women and Śūdras are purified when it has touched the lips even once.
Bathing with mantras addressed to the water-deities, sprinkling [the body], restraint of the breath, worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī; YDh 1.22.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava; this is the threefold restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama). Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.23.
Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water consecrated by the three verses addressed to the waters,
he should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the stars appear in the west.
One should thus stand during the morning twilight until the sun appears, and likewise during the evening twilight;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-ritual at both twilights.
Then he should salute his elders, saying,
"I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study.
When summoned, he should study; whatever he has obtained, he should present to him;
and he should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.27)

Those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, virtuous, and free from envy; who are capable, trustworthy, and givers of knowledge and wealth—such persons should be taught the Dharma by a righteous teacher.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, a sacred thread, and a girdle;
he should go about for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own subsistence. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.29)
The practice of begging for alms by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is characterized by the word *bhavat* at the beginning, middle, and end respectively.

Having performed his fire-rituals, he should eat with speech restrained by the permission of his guru, preceded by the ritual sipping of water (āpośāna), honoring the food and not disparaging it. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.31)
Established in the life of a student (brahmacarya), a Brāhmaṇa shall not eat the food of a single person except in times of distress;
however, he may eat at a funeral feast (śrāddha) as much as he desires, provided he does not violate his vow.
One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food remnants, fermented gruel, women, injury to living beings, gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and the like. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.33)
He who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him is a guru;
he who, having initiated him, gives him the Veda is declared to be an ācārya.
The teacher, the officiating priest, and the one who performs the sacrifice are said to be [the givers] of a single part.
These are to be honored according to their precedence; among them, however, the mother is the most venerable.
The period of studentship for each Veda is twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until the Veda has been mastered, and the tonsure ceremony occurs in the sixteenth year.
The time for initiation for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya classes is until the sixteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth year, respectively. Beyond these, it is no longer permissible.
Henceforth, these people fall from their status, excluded from all religious duties;
they are fallen from the Sāvitrī and become Vratyas, except through the Vratyastoma sacrifice.
Since Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are born once from their mother and a second time from the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, they are therefore remembered as "twice-born."
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good through sacrifices, austerities, and indeed all auspicious actions. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.40)
The twice-born who studies the Rigveda verses every day shall satisfy the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.41)
He who studies the Yajus formulas every day according to his ability gratifies the gods with ghee and nectar, and likewise the ancestors with clarified butter and honey. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.42)
He who recites this every day shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and he shall provide satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and ghee. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.43)
Reciting the Atharva-Angiras texts, the twice-born man should daily gratify the gods with fat and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter, according to his ability. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.44)
For he who daily studies, according to his ability, the dialogues, the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsī verses, the Gāthās, the Itihāsas, and the sciences; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.45.
He provides satisfaction for the gods with meat, milk-rice, and honey;
and he should provide satisfaction for the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.46)
Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires;
whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain the fruit of each one.
The twice-born who is constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) enjoys here the fruit of three gifts of the earth filled with wealth, as well as that of supreme austerity.
But the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher;
in his absence, in the presence of the teacher's son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire.
Wearing away the body by this method, one who has conquered the senses attains the world of Brahmā and is not born again in this world. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.50)
[3. Chapter on Marriage] Having given a gift to the teacher, he should bathe, or do so with his permission;
having brought the Veda, the vows, or indeed both, to completion. Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.51.

Having remained chaste, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks— one who has belonged to no other man before, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.
One should marry a woman who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same ṛṣi-lineage or gotra as oneself,
beyond the fifth degree on the mother's side and likewise beyond the seventh degree on the father's side.
From a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations,
even if it be prosperous, yet not tainted by the defect of hereditary diseases.
A bridegroom of the same caste who possesses these very qualities, who is learned in the Vedas,
carefully examined for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people, is the best.

As for what is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra woman as a wife by those of the twice-born castes—this is not my opinion, because in that case, he himself is born [as a Śūdra]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.56)
Three wives in the order of the castes, two likewise, and one respectively, are the lawful wives for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya; for one born of the Śūdra caste, she alone is his own.
The Brāhma marriage is that in which [the bride] is invited and given, adorned according to one's ability;
the son born of it purifies twenty-one persons on both sides.
The *daiva* marriage is that in which [the bride] is given to an officiating priest at a sacrifice; the *ārṣa*, however, is that in which [the bride] is given after receiving two cows.
The son born of the first [marriage] purifies fourteen generations, and the son born of the latter [purifies] six. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.59)
Having said this, that body which is given to a seeker by one practicing dharma together with her purifies six ancestors, six descendants, and herself. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.60)
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.61)

The hand should be taken in marriage from women of the same caste; however, for the marriage of a twice-born man, a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, and a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a paternal kinsman, and likewise the mother— each subsequent one among these,
provided they are of sound mind, gives the daughter in marriage upon the failure of each preceding one.
By not giving her away at every fertile season, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo;
however, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among eligible suitors.
A maiden is given only once; he who carries her off incurs the punishment of a thief.
Even if she has been given away, one may take her back from the previous husband if a more excellent suitor arrives.
One who gives a girl in marriage without declaring her defects shall be punished with the highest fine;
but one who abandons a faultless girl shall be fined, while one who falsely accuses her of a defect shall be fined one hundred panas.
The *akṣatā* (the one who has not lost her virginity), the *kṣatā* (the one who has been violated), and the *punarbhū* (the remarried woman) who is consecrated again;
and the *svairiṇī* (the wanton woman) who, having abandoned her husband, resorts out of desire to a man of her own caste. *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 1.67.

If a woman is childless, her brother-in-law, with the permission of her elders and desiring a son, or a sapinda or a sagotra, having been anointed with clarified butter, may approach her during her fertile period. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.68)
He may go [to his wife] until the birth of a child; otherwise, he would become fallen. A son born according to this rule is considered his "soil-born" (kṣetraja) son.
He shall cause the unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, wearing soiled garments, subsisting on mere alms, treated with contempt, and sleeping on the ground. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.70)
Soma gave them purity, and Gandharva gave them a beautiful voice; Pāvaka bestowed upon them fitness for all sacrificial rites, for thus women are indeed pure. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.71)
Purification is prescribed after her menstrual period in the event of infidelity;
however, abandonment is ordained if she becomes pregnant, or in cases such as the murder of the fetus or her husband, as well as for other grave sins.

A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, a rogue, one who bears no children, one who wastes her husband's wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly, one who gives birth only to daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband, may be superseded by another wife.
A wife who has been formally accepted must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish.
Whether her husband is dead or alive, she who does not approach another man attains fame in this world and rejoices together with Umā in the next.

If he abandons a wife who is obedient, skillful, the mother of sons, and sweet-spoken, he shall be made to pay a third of his property; if he is destitute, he must provide maintenance for her. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.76)
Wives must carry out the word of their husbands; this is the highest duty of a woman.
For one defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must be awaited until purification.
Because the infinity of worlds and the attainment of heaven through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons depend upon them,
therefore women should be enjoyed and should be well-protected.
The sixteen nights of women are the seasons; among these, he should approach her on the even nights.
He should remain as one practicing celibacy, avoiding the sacred festival days (parvan) and the first four nights.
Proceeding in this manner, he should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla;
when the moon is in its full strength, a man shall once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks.
Or he may act according to his desire, recollecting the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for women are declared to be worthy of protection.
Women should be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, paternal kinsmen, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and other relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food.
With household utensils kept in order, being skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure,
she, devoted to her husband, should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey should abandon play, the adornment of her body, attending social gatherings and festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others.
The father shall protect the maiden; her husband, when she is married; and her sons in old age. In their absence, her kinsmen shall protect her; a woman is never independent. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.85)
She should not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles;
otherwise, she would be censurable even in the absence of her husband.
Devoted to the welfare and pleasure of their husband, well-conducted, and having conquered their senses,
she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death.
If another wife of equal caste exists, one should not have religious duties performed by her;
among wives of equal caste who are eligible for religious rites, none other than the eldest may perform them.
Having cremated a wife of good conduct with the Agnihotra fire, the husband should, without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.89)

[4. Chapter on the Distinction of Color and Birth] From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage; through blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the progeny. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.90)
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born; from a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava is born.

From a Kṣatriya father and Vaiśya or Śūdra mothers, the sons are known as Māhiṣya and Ugra respectively; from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, the son is a Karaṇa. This is the rule declared for women who have been wedded.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
but from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties.
A Vaiśya woman bore a Māgadha to a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra woman bore a Kṣattṛ;
furthermore, a Vaiśya woman begot a son, the Āyogava, from a Śūdra. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.94)
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
these, born from inverse and direct orders, are to be known as both "non-existent" and "existent."
An elevation of caste is to be known as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation;
upon the reversal of actions, there is equality, and the sequence of higher and lower is as previously stated.

[5. The Section on the Duties of the Householder] A householder should perform every day the *smārta* rites in the nuptial fire, or those performed at the time of inheritance; he should perform the *śrauta* rites in the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.97)
Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rites of purification,
the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsaṃdhyā), preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.

Having offered oblations into the fires dedicated to the Sun, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras, master the meaning of the Vedas, and study various treatises. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.99)
And he should approach the Lord for the sake of attaining security and prosperity;
having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship the gods and the ancestors.

To the best of one's ability, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), one should recite the Vedas, the Atharva-veda, the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, and the knowledge concerning the supreme self.

The Bali-offering, the Svadhā-oblation, Vedic study, and the hospitable reception of guests are the great sacrifices to the spirits, the ancestors, the gods, Brahman, and human beings. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.102)
From the remnants of the food offered to the gods, he should present the *bali* offering to the spirits;
he should also place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.103)

Food should be given daily to the ancestors and to men, as well as water; one should constantly perform the private recitation of the Veda, and one should not cook food for oneself alone. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.104)

Having fed the children, the daughters living in the household, the elderly, the pregnant women, the sick, the young girls, the guests, and the servants, the husband and wife should eat the remains. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.105)
A twice-born man eating his food should likewise perform the *āpośana* rite both before and after; thus the food must be made as if not naked and as if it were nectar.
To those of the various social orders, one should give according to one's ability and in due order as guests;
even in the evening, a guest must not be turned away, even if only with kind words, a place to sit, grass, or water.
O monks, alms should be given with respect to one who observes vows;
and one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time.
One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya),
along with hospitable treatment, a seat, delicious food, and pleasant, truthful speech.

But every year, the following are worthy of the guest-offering (arghya): a Snātaka, a teacher, a king, a dear friend, one for whom one’s daughter is being married, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.110)
A traveler and a learned Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas should be known as guests;
these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahmā.
One should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by blameless persons;
one should also avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.112)
He should follow his guest—an accomplished Vedic scholar who has been satisfied—until the boundary of the village;
he should remain with him for the remainder of the day, along with cultured men, beloved friends, and kinsmen.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions, having offered oblations into those fires and attended to them,
and having eaten with his dependents to a moderate degree of satiety, he should then go to sleep.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he should contemplate his own welfare;
he should not neglect virtue, wealth, and pleasure at their proper times, according to his ability. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.115)
They are to be honored in order according to their learning, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves honor on account of his old age. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.116)

Way must be yielded to the elderly, the burdened, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath (snātaka), women, the sick, ascetics, and those who possess a wheel [of sovereignty]; among these, the king is to be honored by them, and the snātaka is to be honored by the king.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are for the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
for the Brāhmaṇa, there are additionally the receiving of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.118)
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
for a Vaiśya, it is traditionally held to be moneylending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born.
Delighting in his wife, pure, supporting his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites,
he should not neglect the five great sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, charity, self-control, compassion, and patience are the means for the practice of dharma for all. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.122)
One should likewise adopt a conduct that is consistent with one's age, intellect, wealth, speech, appearance, learning, birth, and actions— conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit.
A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may indeed drink the Soma;
he whose food supply lasts for one year should perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice.
Every year the Soma sacrifice is to be performed, as well as the animal sacrifice at each solstice;
likewise, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be observed.
In the absence of these, the twice-born should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
one should not perform a rite with deficient materials when the necessary substances are available, for it yields no fruit.
By performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra, one is born as a Cāṇḍāla;
by not giving what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one becomes a vulture or even a crow. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.127)

One may possess grain sufficient for a granary or a jar, or enough for three days, or even not enough for tomorrow; or one may live by gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains—each succeeding mode among these is superior to the preceding.
[6. The Section on the Duties of a Snātaka] He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from any improper source;
he should never indulge in forbidden things, and he should always be contented. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.129)

If he is suffering from hunger, he may seek wealth from kings, pupils, or those for whom he performs sacrifices; however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who rely on fallacious reasoning, heretics, and those who act like herons.
Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails kept short, and being pure,
he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is false, nor should one be a thief or a usurer.
Wearing the sacred thread of a Dakṣāyaṇī, carrying a bamboo staff and a water-pot,
he should circumambulate clockwise the gods, clay, cows, Brahmins, and trees.
But one should not urinate in a river, in shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one face the fire, the sun, a cow, the moon, the twilight, water, a woman, or the twice-born.
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one, while impure, look at urine, feces, or the stars during an eclipse.
Reciting the entire mantra, "This is my vajra," he may go about unsheltered when it rains; however, he should not sleep with his head facing west.
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
nor should one warm one's feet over a fire, nor step over it. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.137)
One should not drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one wake a sleeping person.
One should not play with dice, nor should one lie down with those who destroy dharma or with those who are diseased. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.138)
One should avoid forbidden actions, crossing a river by means of a corpse's smoke, and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, charcoal, or a skull. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.139)
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter through a place other than the gate;
one should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures.
In receiving gifts, the butcher, the wine-seller, the gambler, the prostitute, and the king are wicked;
each of these is ten times more wicked than the one preceding it, respectively.

The commencement of the study of the chapters (of the Veda) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa, or when the herbs have appeared under the asterism Hasta, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the day of Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā,
one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside [the village] near water, according to the prescribed rule.
There is a suspension of study for three days when a disciple, a sacrificial priest, a teacher, or a relative has died;
likewise upon the commencement (upākarmaṇi) and the conclusion (utsarge) of the Vedic term, and when a person learned in one's own Vedic branch (śrotriya) has died.

Upon the occurrence of thunder during twilight, a hurricane, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors, one should complete the study of the Veda for a day and night; likewise, after studying the *Āraṇyaka*, one should do the same. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.145)

On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during an eclipse of Rāhu, at the transitions of the seasons, or after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha) or accepting a gift from such a feast; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.146.

If an animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a mouse passes between [the teacher and the student], there must be a fast for one day and night; the same applies when [a cloud] falls upon Indra (i.e., rains) or rises up.
In the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, or arrows;
near impure substances, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste, a cremation ground, or one who has fallen from his caste; *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 1.148.

In an impure place, or when one is oneself impure; during lightning, thunder, or heavy rain; after eating while the hands are still wet; inside water; at midnight; or during an excessively strong wind—one should not study. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.149)

When there is a rain of dust, a conflagration of the quarters, fear caused by twilight or mist, a foul odor, or when a learned person has come to the house, one should run [to the shelter]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.150)

When there is the sound of a donkey, a camel, a carriage, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; or when trees grow on a barren field—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary times unfit for study.

One should not step on the shadow of a deity, an officiating priest, a *snātaka*, a teacher, or a king; nor should one step on the shadow of another's wife, or on blood, feces, urine, spittle, or the remains of unguents and the like.
Brahmins and Kṣatriyas should never be treated with contempt; until death one should desire prosperity, and one should not touch anyone on their vital spot. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.153)
One should discard remnants of food, excrement, urine, and foot-wash water at a distance;
one should always properly practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.154)
One should not touch cows, Brahmins, fire, or food while impure from eating, nor should one touch them with the foot.
One should not revile or strike them; however, one may strike a son or a pupil.
One should diligently practice dharma through action, mind, and speech;
however, one should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world.
With mother, father, guests, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, maternal uncles, the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and relatives; Yājñavalkya 1.157.
By avoiding disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, offspring, wives, slaves, and kinsmen, a householder shall conquer all the worlds. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.158)
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first removing five lumps [of earth];
however, one may bathe in rivers, natural reservoirs, lakes, and springs.
One should avoid another's bed, seat, garden, house, and vehicle;
and one should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.160)
[One should not eat the food] of misers, prisoners, thieves,
eunuchs, actors, flute-players, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a guild.
One should not accept food from physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, or enemies;
nor from the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātyas, the hypocritical, or those who eat the remnants of others. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.162)

[One should not eat the food] of a woman without a husband, a goldsmith, a woman who has conquered her village [by witchcraft], a sacrificer for a village, a seller of weapons, a blacksmith, a weaver, or one who lives by dogs. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.163)

[One should not eat the food] of a cruel man, a king, a washerman, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter, a laundryman, a vintner, or those who live with a paramour in the same house. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.164)
The food of the slanderer and the liar, as well as that of jugglers and bards, and likewise that of those who sell Soma, must not be eaten. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.165)

Among Śūdras, those who are slaves, cowherds, family friends, or sharecroppers, as well as barbers and one who offers himself [as a servant], are persons whose food may be eaten. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.166)

[7. Section on Edible and Non-edible Food] Food that has not been honored, meat not intended for sacrifice, food containing hair or insects, that which has turned sour, stale food, leavings, food touched by a dog, or food looked upon by an outcaste; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.167.
One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food announced [beforehand], and food served in rotation;
as well as food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, and that which has been intentionally touched with the foot.
Food that has become stale may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat, even if it has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil or fat.

One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or one that is nursing; likewise, the milk of camels, of single-hoofed animals, of women, of wild animals, and of sheep. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.170)

One should avoid sacrificial offerings intended for the gods, the śigru plant, red exudations from incisions, meat not consecrated by ritual slaughter, substances produced in dung, and mushrooms. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.171)
Flesh-eating birds, the dātyūha, parrots, peckers, ṭiṭṭibhas, cranes, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds [should not be eaten].
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, and baka birds, as well as grain-scatterers;
and [forbidden] preparations made without purpose, such as kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī.
The kalaviṅka, the kākola, the kurara, the rajjudālaka,
web-footed birds, the khañjarīṭa, and wild animals and birds that are unknown.
Having eaten blue jays, red-footed birds,
dog meat, dried meat, or fish out of desire, one shall dwell for three days observing a fast.
Having eaten onion, village-pig, mushroom, village-cock, garlic, or leek, one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.176)
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the pangolin, and the hare are edible;
and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita are indeed fit for consumption.
Likewise, the pāṭhīna, rājīva, and scaled fish may be eaten by the twice-born;
therefore, hear now the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.178)

In a life-threatening emergency, at a śrāddha ceremony, when meat has been consecrated with water (prokṣita), or at the request of a Brahmin—having duly honored the gods and ancestors—one who eats meat incurs no fault. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.179)
That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the bodies of those animals. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.180)
By abstaining from meat, a Brahmin who is a sage, even while dwelling at home, attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.181)

[8. Chapter on the Purification of Substances] Regarding gold, silver, lotuses, vessels with raised rims, and stones; vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and skins; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.182.
The purification of vessels and cups is held to be by means of water;
however, vessels for the *caru* oblation, the *sruk*, and the *sruva* ladles that have been smeared with fat are purified with hot water.

The sprinkling with water (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed for the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the skin (ajina), grains, the pestle (musala), the mortar (ulūkhala), and the fire-drill wood (araṇi); as well as for large quantities of grains and garments that are kept together in a heap.
Wooden, horn, and bone vessels are to be scraped; those made of fruit are to be scrubbed with cow-hair;
and sacrificial implements used in the ritual act are to be wiped with the hand.
Woolen cloth and silk are purified with saline water and cow's urine;
fine cotton cloth with *śrīphala* fruits, and likewise *kutapa* wool with *ariṣṭa* fruits.

Linen cloth purified by white mustard seeds, earthenware by being fired again, the hand of an artisan, merchandise, alms-food, and likewise the mouth of a woman—these are pure. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.187)
The purification of the ground is achieved by sweeping, burning, the passage of time, the treading of cows, sprinkling, scraping, and smearing;
likewise, a house is purified by sweeping and smearing.
When food has been smelled by a cow, or is defiled by hair, flies, or insects,
water, ashes, or even earth should be thrown into it for the sake of purification.
The purification of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, and water; that of bell-metal and iron is with ashes and water; and for liquids, it is by means of immersion.
The purification of an object smeared with impurities is by means of earth and water until the odor and other traces are removed;
that which is commended by word, that which is washed with water, and that which is unknown [to be defiled] are always pure.
Water on the ground that is naturally pure and sufficient for one's thirst is clean;
likewise is meat fallen from the jaws of dogs, Cāṇḍālas, carnivorous animals, and the like. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.192)
A ray of light, fire, dust, shade, a cow, a horse, the earth, and wind;
droplets and flies are pure when touched, and a calf is pure when it causes the flow of milk.
The mouths of goats and horses are pure, but not those of cows or humans; these are impure.
And roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.194)

Drops from the mouth are pure, as are drops from the water used for sipping; likewise, the beard that enters the mouth is pure, and one becomes pure after spitting out what is stuck between the teeth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.195)
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, walked upon a road, or changed one's garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again. Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.196.
The muddy waters of a street that have been touched by outcasts, dogs,
or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are those collected from bricks that have been fired.

[9. The Section on Giving] Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of Dharma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.198)
The Brahmins who are devoted to sacred learning and study are the source of all;
among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and even more excellent than they are those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self.
Neither by learning alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient;
rather, that in whom both of these, as well as good conduct, reside is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.200)
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth, should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise man desiring his own welfare. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.201)
A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
for by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.202)
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions;
even when asked, one should give with faith and according to one's ability.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, well-tempered and covered with cloth,
accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee, should be given as a gift.
The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is tawny (kapilā), she further delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation.

By giving a cow that yields milk from both teats along with her calf, according to the previously mentioned rite, the donor attains heaven for as many yugas as there are hairs on the bodies of the two.
As long as both the feet and the face of the calf are visible within the womb,
so long is the cow to be known as the Earth, until she releases the fetus.
Having given a cow, whether it be a milch-cow or even one that is not, in whatever manner possible—
provided it is healthy and free from blemish— the donor is glorified in heaven.

Massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away their leavings are equal to the gift of a cow. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.209)
By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter,
a dwelling, gold, and draft animals, one is glorified in heaven.
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella, a garland, ointment, a vehicle, a tree, a beloved [object], or a bed, one becomes supremely happy. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.211)
Since Brahman consists of all dharmas and is superior to all gifts,
one who gives that attains the imperishable world of Brahman.
Even though he is capable of accepting gifts,
he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds that belong to those whose nature is charity.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, roasted grain, and water—these should not be refused. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.214)
One may accept food brought unasked even from a person of evil deeds, except in the case of an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.215)
For the sake of honoring the gods and guests, for the purpose of serving his teacher, or indeed for his own subsistence, he may accept gifts from anyone at all. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.216)

[10. Chapter on Faithful Offerings (Śrāddhaprakaraṇam)] The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, the occasion of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices, the availability of materials, the excellence of Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun’s transit. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.217)
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the proper times for a śrāddha.

The foremost among all those learned in the Vedas, a śrotriya who knows Brahman, a youth, one who understands the meaning of the Vedas, a master of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, one who knows the Trimadhu and the Trisuparṇa; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.219.

A sister’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, one for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, one who has kindled the three *nāciketa* fires, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman; [these are those with whom one may eat]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.220)

Those Brahmins who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong students, and those who are devoted to their fathers and mothers, are the ones who bring success to the Śrāddha.

One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is blind in one eye, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; YDh 1.222.

One who teaches for wages, a eunuch, a defiler of virgins, one accused of a grave crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.223.

Those who abandon their mother, father, or guru; those who eat the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala* (a Śūdra); the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.
On the day before [the ceremony], the self-possessed and pure host should invite the Brāhmaṇas;
they too must remain restrained in their mental, vocal, and physical actions. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.225)
Having honored those who have arrived with a welcome in the afternoon, he,
with purified hands, should cause them to sit upon their seats after they have sipped water for ritual purification.
One should invite an even number of guests for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors;
this should be done in a purified place that is well-spread and slopes toward the south.
Two [seats] for the gods are placed to the east; three for the ancestors to the north, or even one for each;
and the same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common offering (tantra).

Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O All-Gods" (*viśve devāsaḥ*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.229)
Then, having scattered barley grains over a vessel containing a strainer,
he should pour water with the verse *śaṃ no devīr* and likewise barley grains with the formula *yavo 'si*.
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should pour the *arghya* water into their hands;
having given water, fragrance, garlands, incense, and a lamp. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.231)
Likewise, he should give a garment and water for the purpose of washing the hands;
then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should perform the circumambulation of the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction (apradakṣiṇa).

Having offered double-folded kuśa grass and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uṣantas tvā," he should, being permitted by them, recite thereafter: "May they come to us. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.233)
Having scattered sesame seeds all around with the words "apahatāḥ," one should perform the functions of barley with sesame seeds and offer the *arghya* and other honors as before.

Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule, he turns the vessel face down with the words, "Thou art the seat of the ancestors. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.235)
Intending to offer [the food] into the fire, he takes up the food soaked in ghee and asks, "Do you perform [the offering]?
Having been authorized with the words "Do so," he offers it into the fire according to the ritual for the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
With a concentrated mind, he should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels as they are available,
especially those made of silver.
Having given the food, he should consecrate the vessel with the mantra "The earth is the vessel";
then, having recited "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should cause the thumb of the twice-born guest to touch the food.
Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyahṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as necessary for comfort.
Free from anger and without haste, he should give food that is desirable and fit for oblation;
and until [the guests] are satisfied, he should mutter purifying mantras as well as the previously mentioned prayers.
Having taken food and being satisfied, and having obtained permission regarding the remainder,
one should scatter that food on the ground and offer water once for each [deceased ancestor].
Taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south,
he should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
In the same manner, one should likewise offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the maternal grandfathers;
then one should perform the recitation of the Svasti formula and the offering of the inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka).

Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*. Being permitted with the words "Let it be recited," he should say to those present, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.244)
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should then pour water on the ground;
when the Brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should mutter this: (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.245).
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.246)
Having spoken thus and having uttered pleasant words, he should bow down and dismiss [the guests] with the words "vāje vāje," being joyful; the dismissal is performed starting with the ancestors.
But having turned face upwards that vessel of the ancestors into which the remnants were previously placed in the *arghya* vessel, one should dismiss the Brahmins. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.248)
Having circumambulated [the vessel] clockwise, he should eat what was partaken of by the ancestors;
he should observe celibacy for that night together with the Brahmins.
Thus, moving clockwise for the sake of prosperity, one should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors with offerings of balls of rice mixed with curd and jujube fruits, and perform the rites using barley.
The Ekoddiṣṭa rite is devoid of the gods, with only one offering of water (arghya) and one purifying blade of grass (pavitraka);
it is indeed performed without the invocation (āvāhana) and the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
At the dismissal of the Brahmins, he should say "May you be satisfied" at the place where the water-offering was made;
they should reply, "We are indeed satisfied. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.252)

One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of the *arghya* offering; one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.253)
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," he should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for a single person (ekoddiṣṭa) applies to women as well. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.254)
For one whose *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has taken place before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born for the duration of that year.
On the anniversary of the day of death, the rite should be performed every month for a year, and likewise annually thereafter; however, the first rite is to be performed on the eleventh day.
One should give the morsels of food to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else cast them into fire or water;
while worthy Brahmins are present, one must not clear away the leavings of the twice-born.

One [attains the same merit] by means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year; likewise by the meat of fish, deer, antelope, birds, goat, and spotted deer. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.258)
By offering the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively,
the ancestors here are satisfied for an increasing number of months with each successive month.
The flesh of the rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, honey, or the food of sages;
the flesh of iron-eating insects, large vegetables, and the meat of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane.
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
A daughter, those who seek a daughter, cattle, virtuous sons, as well as gambling, agriculture, trade, and animals with cloven and uncloven hooves; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.262.
The giver of the Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic splendor, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desires. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.263)
On the days beginning with the first of the lunar fortnight, excluding the fourteenth,
offerings are made there for those who have indeed been slain by weapons.
For one obtains heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength, as well as a preeminent son, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, and auspiciousness. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.265)
As well as the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], commerce and other such pursuits,
freedom from disease, fame, the absence of sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly offers the Śrāddha ceremony bestows wealth, the Vedas, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.268)
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
when satiated by the śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
When pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men long life, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.270)

[11. The Section on the Ritual of Gaṇapati] Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā for the purpose of accomplishing tasks and removing obstacles, as well as for the lordship over the hosts (gaṇas). Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.271.
Learn now the symptoms of one who is afflicted by that [demon]:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.272)
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he dwells together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels.
Even while walking, he thinks himself followed by others;
dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he sinks down without apparent cause.
Afflicted by that [evil eye], the prince does not obtain the kingdom; the maiden does not find a husband, and the woman does not obtain offspring or a fetus. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.275)

The teacher does not attain the status of an ācārya, nor does the learned brahmin obtain discipleship; likewise, the student does not achieve mastery of his studies, the merchant gains no profit, and the farmer reaps no success from his cultivation.
On an auspicious day, his ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed according to the prescribed rules,
after he has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Likewise, for one whose head has been anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, virtuous brahmins should pronounce the benediction of "Svasti."
One should throw into the water earth from a horse stable, an elephant stable, an anthill, a confluence, and a lake,
as well as yellow pigment, perfumes, and guggulu resin.
Having brought [the water] from the lake in four jars of a single color,
one should then place the auspicious seat upon the hide of a red bull.
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, made purifying by the seers—with that I sprinkle you; may the *pāvamānī* verses purify you. (Yajurveda 1.281)
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the Seven Seers grant you fortune.
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, in the parting of your hair, or on your head; whatever is in your forehead, your ears, or your eyes—may the waters destroy that forever. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.283)
Having bathed, he should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood upon his head,
while grasping kusha grass with his left hand.
And likewise with *mita*, *sammita*, *śālakaṭaṅkaṭa*, *kūśmāṇḍa*, and *rājaputra*, each accompanied by *svāhā* at the end. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.285)
Having spread *kuśa* grass on all sides upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, he should offer [the oblation] with their names and with *bali*-mantras accompanied by salutations.
Rice that has been husked and unhusked, as well as rice mixed with meat broth, cooked fish and likewise raw fish, and meat—only these [are permitted]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.287)
Variegated and fragrant flowers, as well as the three kinds of liquor, radishes, fried cakes, sweetmeats, and garlands of *uṇḍeraka*— these he should offer.
Having collected all of these— curd-rice, milk-rice, and flour-cakes with molasses along with water— and having placed them upon the ground, he should then place his head there.
Then he should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka,
having offered a full añjali of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers as an arghya.
Grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me fortune;
grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires.
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
he should feed the Brahmins and also give a pair of garments to his preceptor.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By constantly performing worship of the Sun, as well as the *tilaka* of his Lord and that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain perfection.

[12. The Section on the Pacification of Planets] One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, and nourishment, or likewise one performing malevolent rites, should perform the sacrifice to the planets. Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.295.
The Sun, the Moon, the Son of Earth (Mars), the Son of Soma (Mercury), Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu are known as the planets.
The planets should be fashioned, in order, from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal.
They should be depicted on a cloth with their own respective colors, or [represented] by fragrances in mandalas;
and garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors.
Fragrances, offerings, and incense of guggulu should be presented;
and oblations accompanied by mantras must be performed for each respective deity.
The verses beginning with "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed to be used in their respective order. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.300)
"Bṛhaspate ati yat aryaḥ," likewise "annāt parisrutaḥ," "śaṃ no devīḥ," likewise "kāṇḍāt," and "ketuṃ kṛṇvan imān" likewise.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, then pippala, udumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in their respective order. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.302)
For each [deity], however, one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations should be offered,
mixed with honey and clarified butter, or with curd or milk.
Rice cooked with molasses, milk-rice, sacrificial food, rice with milk and ṣaṣṭika grain, rice with curd, clarified butter, flour, meat, and variegated rice. Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.304.
In this manner, a wise man should provide food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets,
honoring them with due ceremony and according to his ability or as it may be obtained, in accordance with the prescribed rule.
A cow, a conch, likewise a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, in order: a black cow, iron, and a goat—these indeed are recorded as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
And whoever is in distress due to another at any time should honor that person with effort;
for this boon was granted to them by Brahmā: "When you are honored, you shall honor [others] in return. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.307)
The rise and fall of kings, as well as the existence and non-existence of the world, are dependent upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
One should perform this hospitality for the planets even once a year;
endowed with health and strength, he shall live for a hundred autumns. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.308)
[13. Chapter on the Duties of Kings] One who possesses great energy, is liberal, grateful, and serves the elderly;
who is disciplined, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure—YDh 1.309.
One who is not dilatory, possessed of mindfulness, not mean-spirited, nor harsh;
likewise righteous, free from vices, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.310)

That lord of men was likewise trained in the protection of his own vulnerabilities through the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī) and the science of government (daṇḍanīti), as well as in the science of economics (vārtā) and the triple Vedic knowledge (trayī).
He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
with them he should deliberate upon the kingdom, and thereafter with a Brahmin, and finally by himself. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.312)
He should appoint as his domestic priest one who is well-known for his learning, skilled in astrology,
proficient in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda].
And for the sake of performing rites prescribed by revelation and tradition,
he should indeed choose officiating priests and should likewise perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
And he should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings.
That which is poured from the fire into the fire of a Brahmin—unspilled, undisturbed, and untainted by expiatory rites—is declared here to be the most excellent. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.316)
One should seek what has not been obtained through righteous means; what has been obtained, one should protect with effort;
what has been protected, one should increase through prudent policy; and what has been increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients.
Having granted land or having established a fixed endowment, the king should cause a written deed to be made for the information of future benevolent rulers. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.318)
On a cloth or a copper plate, the lord of the earth, having inscribed his own lineage and himself, marked with his own seal above; YDh 1.319.
One should cause a stable edict to be issued, specifying the dimensions of the land received, describing the boundaries of the gift, and completed with one's own hand and the date.

He should dwell in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the protection of his people, his treasury, and himself. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.321)
And in each of those matters, he should appoint supervisors who are proficient, skilled, pure,
and diligent in the affairs of revenue and expenditure.
There is no higher duty for kings than this: that wealth acquired in battle is given to the Brahmins, and constant fearlessness is granted to the subjects. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.323)
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land,
without turning their backs and with weapons free from deceit, go to heaven just like yogins.

The king takes away the merit of those who do not retreat when their ranks are broken, as well as the steps [of those] slain while fleeing, which are equal to the merit of a sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.325)

One should not strike one who proclaims "I am yours," a eunuch, one who is unarmed, one who has joined another's side, one who has turned away from battle, or one who is merely looking on at the fight. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.326)
Having performed the protective rites, he should rise and personally inspect income and expenditure;
thereafter, having attended to legal affairs and bathed, he may eat according to his desire.
He should have the gold brought by the attendants deposited in the treasuries;
thereafter, having consulted with his ministers, he should inspect the secret agents and dispatch messengers.
Then he may move about at his own will, or associate with his ministers;
having inspected his forces, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he may enjoy himself with songs and dances, and he should also recite his sacred study.
He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise wake up to them;
he should reflect with his intellect upon the scriptures as well as all his duties.

Then, having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the domestic chaplain, and the teachers, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and among others. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.332)
Having seen [the results], he should give cows, gold, and land to the astrologers and physicians;
furthermore, he should give houses and dwellings to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward those who are affectionate, and wrathful toward his enemies;
he should behave toward his circle of servants and his subjects like a father.
Protecting [them] according to the law, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for the protection of subjects is superior to all other forms of giving. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.335)
He shall protect the subjects from being oppressed by flatterers, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like, and especially from scribes.
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected, half of that belongs to the king, because he receives taxes from them. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.337)
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed to govern the realm,
the king should honor the virtuous and have those who act contrary to them executed.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
he should always cause learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) to dwell [in his realm], honoring them with gifts, respect, and hospitality. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.339)
The king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means shall, before long, lose his royal fortune and meet with destruction along with his kinsmen.
The fire born from the suffering and oppression of the subjects does not cease until it has consumed the king’s lineage, his fortune, and his very life.
Whatever duty belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,
that same duty in its entirety he obtains when bringing another's kingdom under his control.
In whatever country there is a particular custom, legal practice, or family tradition,
that very same thing must be maintained when one has come under its influence.
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, he should keep his counsel well-guarded, so that others do not know it until the results of his actions have come to fruition. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.344)
The enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, the one beyond him, and the one further still—
this circle of states should be considered in their proper order and approached with diplomatic means such as conciliation and the rest.
The expedients of conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise force, when properly employed, may achieve success; yet force is the last resort when no other way remains.
He should duly deliberate upon these strategic qualities: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and the double policy.
One should march against a foreign kingdom when it is endowed with the excellence of crops,
while the enemy is weak and one's own mounts and men are joyful.
The accomplishment of action is established upon both destiny and human effort;
therein, destiny is that which was manifested through human effort in a previous life.

Some of virtuous intellect maintain that the fruit [of action] arises from destiny, others from inherent nature, some from time, and others from human effort; while some desire it to arise from the combination of these.
For just as a chariot cannot move with only one wheel, so destiny does not succeed without human effort. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.351)
Since the acquisition of friends is superior to the acquisition of gold or land,
one should strive to attain that and, with a concentrated mind, protect the truth.
The sovereign, the ministers, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Having obtained that [kingly power], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.354)
He cannot be led away by right means by one who is greedy, of unrefined intellect, though he be truthful to his word, pure, well-assisted, and wise. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.355)
When employed according to the scriptures, it brings joy to the entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it would provoke their wrath. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.356)
Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
however, proper punishment brings a king heaven, fame, and victory. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.357)

Whether it be a brother, a son, one worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle—there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is not subject to punishment by the king. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.358)
That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and duly executes those deserving of death has performed sacrifices completed with the most excellent sacrificial fees. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.359)
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine the legal cases daily, each separately, as they yield fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.

Having disciplined those who have deviated from their own duty—whether they belong to families, castes, guilds, assemblies, or even rural districts—the king shall establish them on the right path. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.361)
A mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.362)
Three *gauras* make one *yava*; three of those middle-sized *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five of those *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.
Four or five *suvarṇas* are proclaimed to be one *pala*;
two *kṛṣṇalas* make one silver *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *dharaṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, and ten [of those] make one *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*; a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika* is called a *paṇa*.
A fine of eighty-one thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle amercement, and half of that again is recorded as the lowest.

Now, the punishment of reproach, the punishment of speech, the punishment of fines, and likewise corporal punishment—these should be applied either individually or collectively, according to the nature of the offense. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.367)
Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength,
as well as the age, the action, and the wealth [of the offender], he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
[End of the Ācārādhyāya] [II. Vyavahārādhyāya] [1. Sādhāraṇavyavahāramātṛkāprakaraṇam] (The General Section on the Framework of Legal Procedure)
Free from anger and greed, the king should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the treatises on Dharma.

The king should appoint as members of his court those who are accomplished in sacred learning and study, who know the Dharma, who speak the truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.2)
But when the king, due to the pressure of business, is unable to personally oversee legal proceedings,
he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws to preside over them together with the court members.
Whether out of passion, greed, or even fear, those members of the court who act contrary to the law or forget their duty shall each be punished with a fine double that of the litigant.
When one who has not been overcome by others through a path devoid of mindfulness and right conduct brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a ground for legal dispute.
The defendant shall write down, in the presence of the plaintiff, exactly what has been stated by the plaintiff,
marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other identifying characteristics.
The answer to the meaning of what was heard should be written down in the presence of the plaintiff;
thereafter, the defendant shall immediately set forth the proof for the matter he has asserted.
Upon the establishment of that, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
This four-footed procedure has been set forth for the purpose of legal disputes.
[2. Chapter on the Special Categories of Legal Procedure] One should not bring a counter-accusation against someone without having first resolved one's own charge;
nor should one, by means of another, alter the nature of what has been stated by the accused. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.9)
In cases of mutual assault and in matters of violence, one may bring a counter-charge;
in both instances, a surety capable of standing for the decision of the case must be taken.
If he denies it, he should pay the debt to the creditor and an equal amount to the king;
if he makes a false accusation, he shall pay double the amount of the claim as a fine.

In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations regarding a cow, or a woman, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately; in other matters, the time for litigation is said to depend on one's own discretion.
He goes from one place to another, licks the corners of his mouth, his forehead perspires, and his face becomes discolored. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.13)
With speech faltering as it dries up, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor [the guest] with his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.14)
If one undergoes a change from their natural disposition through actions of mind, speech, or body—
whether in a legal proceeding or as a witness— they are proclaimed to be wicked.
He who, being independent, attempts to prove a doubtful matter, he who absconds,
or he who says nothing when summoned, is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment.
When there are witnesses on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff;
but when the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant.
If the dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine, his own wager, and the debt to the creditor. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.18)
Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the truth;
for even the truth, if not presented, is lost in a lawsuit. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.19)

If a defendant denies a written document, but is proven in one part of it, he must be made by the king to pay the entire debt; however, that which was not declared [in court] shall not be accepted as evidence.
When there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, the principle that prevails in practice is this:
the Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative than the Arthaśāstra. This is the established rule. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 2.21)
Written documents, possession, and witnesses are proclaimed as the means of proof;
in the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
In all disputes concerning property, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful.
For land that is being enjoyed by another, there is loss of ownership after twenty years for one who sees it but does not speak;
for property, the loss occurs after ten years. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.24)

Except for property deposited within the boundary, the wealth of the mentally disabled and children, as well as the wealth of deposits, the king’s women, and Vedic scholars (śrotriya). Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.25.
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates deposits and other such items to pay the wealth to the owner,
and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity.
Title-deed is superior to possession, except in the case of property inherited through prior succession;
even when there is a title-deed, it has no force at all where there is not even a small amount of possession. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.27)
But he by whom the title-deed was executed, being summoned, shall produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more authoritative.
If one who was accused should have died, his heir shall clear him;
in that case, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of a legal title (āgama). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.29)

Guilds, corporations, and families appointed by the king—among these, each preceding one is to be understood as more authoritative than the following in the legal procedure for men. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.30)

One should set aside legal proceedings that have arisen through the influence of force, as well as those conducted by women, at night, inside a house, outside [the court], or by enemies. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.31)
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, distressed, a child, or terrified,
as well as one that is incoherent, is not valid.
Property lost and subsequently recovered must be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership through identifying marks, he deserves a fine equal to the value of that property.

Having found a treasure-trove, the king shall give half to the twice-born; the twice-born man, however, if he is learned, may take it all, since he is the master of everything. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.34)
If a treasure is found by someone other than the rightful heir, the king shall take a sixth part;
if the finder has not reported it and is subsequently discovered, he shall be made to pay that [treasure] as well as a fine.
The king must restore property stolen by thieves to the person of the realm;
for by not restoring it, he incurs the same guilt as the thief.
[3. Chapter on the Non-payment of Debt] Interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.37)
But those traveling through a wilderness shall pay ten percent, and those traveling by sea a hundred percent;
or all may pay interest as agreed upon by themselves, regardless of their respective castes.
The interest on the value of livestock and female slaves is eightfold;
that on clothes, grain, and gold is respectively fourfold, threefold, and twofold. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.39)
One who, having approached [the court], is proving his case shall not be censured by the king;
but one who, while being tried, goes to the king [to complain], shall be fined and made to pay that wealth.
A debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they presented their claims;
however, after having paid the Brāhmaṇas, he must pay the king immediately thereafter.
The king shall compel the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount recovered;
and the creditor who has obtained his due shall be made to pay five percent.
