One may compel a person of low birth who has become impoverished to perform labor for the sake of repaying a debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.
If one does not accept their own lent capital when it is being returned,
provided it has been deposited with a neutral third party, it shall not increase beyond that point.
If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided,
the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad.
A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife or son, nor shall he pay one contracted by his son;
likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, except for what was incurred for the sake of the family.

A son shall not pay his father's debts incurred for liquor, desire, gambling, fines, or court fees, nor those remaining after the payment of such, nor debts for useless gifts; these are not paternal obligations he must discharge. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.47)
The husband shall pay the debt of a cowherd, a vintner, an actor, a washerman, or a hunter’s wife,
because their livelihood depends upon him.
A woman shall pay a debt that was contracted by her husband, or one that she herself incurred while acting with him; she is not liable for any other debt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.49)
When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; even if it was denied, it is established by witnesses.
The heir to the estate shall be made to pay the debt, as shall the one who takes the wife;
likewise, the son whose property is not dependent on others shall pay for his father who leaves no heirs.
Furthermore, it is traditionally held that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son,
standing as a surety, contracting debt, or acting as a witness is not permitted so long as they have not divided their inheritance.
Suretyship is prescribed for appearance, for testimony, and for payment;
however, in the case of the first two being rendered false, the debt must be paid by them, and in the case of the latter, even their sons may be liable.

Where a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) must pay it.
If there should be many sureties who provide the debt with their own shares,
the creditor may deal with those who stand under a single liability as he pleases.
But whatever wealth of the creditor a surety is compelled to pay publicly,
that shall be repayable by the debtors to him at double the amount.
In the case of female offspring and livestock, the interest is equal to the principal; grain is said to be tripled, cloth quadrupled, and liquids likewise eightfold.
A pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, provided it is not released;
however, a pledge for a fixed term expires at the end of that time, whereas a pledge to be enjoyed for its produce is never forfeited.
No interest shall accrue on a pledge when it has been used by the creditor, nor when it is damaged or lost;
nor shall he be liable for its loss or destruction, except when caused by an act of God or the king.
If, after the pledge has been accepted, it becomes worthless even while being protected, another pledge may be taken;
or else the debtor shall pay the value, or the creditor shall become the owner of the property.
He shall cause the debtor to pay back with interest the money for which a pledge was made by way of a contract;
however, he shall cause the payment of double the value for goods delivered as a *satyaṅkāra* (token of good faith).

When the debtor has arrived, the pledge must be released; otherwise, he would become a thief. If the creditor is absent, one should deposit the money with the family and recover the pledge. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.62)
Or it may remain there at its value fixed at that time, without interest;
or, with the consent of the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
But when the debt has doubled on the pledge,
then indeed the pledge must be released once the money produced from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and become double [the original loan].

The Section on Deposits (Upanidhi-prakaraṇam)] When an object is placed in another's hand without describing its specific characteristics and remains in the form of a deposit, that is termed *aupanidhika*; it must be returned in exactly that same manner.
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate (such as fire or flood), or by thieves;
however, if it is lost while being sought and not returned, he shall be made to pay [the value] and a fine equal to that amount.
One who lives by his own will shall be punished and made to pay that [debt] along with interest;
this same rule applies to borrowed goods, items held for safekeeping, deposits, and so forth.
[5. Chapter on Witnesses] Those who are ascetic, charitable by nature, of noble birth, speakers of truth, devoted to dharma, upright, having sons, and endowed with wealth; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.68.

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites; they are prescribed according to their respective classes and castes, or all may serve for all.
Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused, performers on stage, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired faculties; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.70.
Outcasts, relatives, those with a financial interest in the case, associates, enemies, thieves, those who commit violence,
and those whose guilt has been proven— these, and others such as those previously excluded, are not to be accepted as witnesses.
Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is approved by both parties;
however, in cases of adultery, theft, verbal abuse, and violence, everyone may be a witness.
He should cause the witnesses, who stand in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, to hear [the following]:
"Those worlds which are for the perpetrators of sins, as well as for those who commit the great sins (mahāpātaka). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.73)
Whatever worlds belong to those who set fires and to those who kill women and children, all of those he attains who gives false testimony. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.74)
Whatever merit has been performed by you over hundreds of previous births, know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.75)
For if men fail to give testimony regarding a debt along with its tenfold interest, the king shall cause them to pay the whole amount on the forty-sixth day. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.76)
For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the facts], is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.77)

In a case of division between two groups, the testimony of the majority prevails; if the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities; and if there is a division even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most excellent in virtue must be accepted.
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
for him who asserts otherwise, defeat is certain.
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous,
or twice as many, should state it otherwise, the former witnesses shall be considered perjured.
The forger and the witnesses shall each be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, and it is ordained that a Brāhmaṇa shall be banished.
He who, having been made to hear the testimony from others, conceals it, being shrouded in darkness, shall be compelled to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should banish.
In a case where the death of those belonging to the [four] castes would otherwise occur, one may give false testimony;
to purify that act, the twice-born must offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.83)

Section on Documents] Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement between the parties, a document should be executed with witnesses, beginning with the name of the creditor. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.84)

It should be marked with the year, month, half-month, day, name, caste, one's own lineage (gotra), fellow-student (sabrahmacārin), one's own [name], and the names of one's father and so forth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.85)
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall record his own name by his own hand, stating: "This which is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.86)
And the witnesses, being equal [in number], shall each write by their own hand, preceded by the name of their father, "I, so-and-so, am a witness here. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.87)
Then, at the end, the scribe should write: "This has been written by me, [Name], the son of [Name], having been requested by both parties. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.88)
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is considered valid evidence, except when it was produced by force or fraud. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.89)
A debt recorded in writing must be paid by three generations of persons;
however, the pledge is enjoyed only so long as that debt has not been discharged.
If a document is located in another country, is difficult to read, lost, rubbed out, stolen, torn, burnt,
or otherwise destroyed, one should have another document prepared.
The validity of a doubtful document may be established by means of a handwriting sample written by the party himself and so forth,
as well as through reasoning, acquisition, performance, marks, connection, and traditional transmission.
The debtor, having paid the money, should write on the back of the document each time a payment is made;
or the creditor, when the debt has been settled, should deliver the document marked with his own hand.
Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or else have another executed for the sake of clarity;
or if the original were witnessed, that [new] document must be executed with witnesses as well. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.94)
The Section on Ordeals] The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals here for the sake of purification;
these are used in cases of grave accusation when the accuser has placed his head upon the stake. *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 2.95.
Or, by mutual consent, one may perform the work while the other provides the head;
even without the head, one may perform it in cases of treason against the king or for a mortal sin.
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on,
he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and the Brahmins.
For women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick, the ordeal shall be by the balance;
for a Śūdra, by fire or water; or for seven barley grains of poison.

One should not carry a plowshare, nor poison, nor a scale for less than a thousand [palas]; however, for the sake of the king’s business or in cases of formal accusation, they may carry these, remaining always pure.

The person who has taken his stand upon the scales, having been examined by experts skilled in weighing, shall be made equal to the counter-weights; then, a mark being made, he shall be lowered from the scales.
O Tula, you were created of old by the gods as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak that truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.101)
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the balance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.102)
Then, having observed that his hands have been rubbed with rice grains,
he should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread for that same duration.
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins. (Yajurveda 2.104)
When he has spoken thus, one should place upon both his hands an iron ball weighing fifty palas, heated to the color of fire.
Taking that [fire], he should walk slowly for exactly seven circumambulations;
each circumambulation should be known to be sixteen finger-breadths in width, with an interval of the same measure.
Having released the fire, if he has not been burnt and the grain has been crushed, he attains purification;
if the ball falls in between or if there is doubt, he should take it up again.

Having sworn an oath over water with the words, "O Varuṇa, protect me by truth," he should seize the knees of one standing in water reaching up to the navel and cause him to drink the water. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.108)
If another swift man, having brought back the arrow shot simultaneously,
should see the man's body submerged when he has departed, he shall obtain purification.
O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness;
protect me from this curse, and by truth become nectar for me. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.110)
Having spoken thus, he should consume the Śārṅga poison born of the snowy mountains;
if it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare him pure. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.111)
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having poured it out, one should then make [the patient] drink three handfuls of that water. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.112)
If a terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone before the fourteenth day, he shall be considered innocent; of this there is no doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.113)

[8. Chapter on the Division of Inheritance] If the father should make a division, he may divide the sons according to his will; either by giving the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114)

If he should divide the shares equally, the wives must be made equal sharers, provided that no separate woman’s property (strīdhana) has been given to them by the husband or by the father-in-law. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.115)
If a capable person does not desire [to divide], a separate arrangement may be made by giving something;
for those divided unequally, the distribution made by the father is remembered as lawful.
After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.
The daughters shall inherit what remains after the debt has been cleared; in their absence, the succession passes to the next of kin.
Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without using paternal property, as well as what is obtained through friendship or marriage, shall not belong to the heirs. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.118)
If one recovers property that was taken away but had come into his possession by succession, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning.
When the property arises as a common whole, the division is traditionally held to be equal;
however, for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is determined according to the father.
Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, or a legal endowment, or even property itself, the ownership therein belongs equally to both the father and the son. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.121)
A son born after the partition of the estate from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share;
or that share may be determined from the visible assets, after deducting the income and expenses.
Whatever has been given to him by his parents shall be his own property;
when they divide [the estate] after the father's death, the mother shall also receive an equal share. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.123)
But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having received a fourth part from their own share, [should be so consecrated]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.124)
The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, shall receive four, three, two, and one shares;
those born of a Kṣatriya shall receive three, two, and one shares; and those born of a Vaiśya shall receive two and one shares. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.125)
If any property that was taken from one another is discovered after the partition has been made, they shall divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule.
A son begotten by appointment upon the wife of a man who has no son belongs,
according to the law, to the inheritance of both [the husband and the progenitor], and he is the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for both.
The legitimate son (aurasa) is one born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra).
The son of the field (kṣetraja), however, is one begotten by a kinsman of the same lineage or by another man upon the wife.
A son born secretly in the house is known as a *gūḍhaja* (secret-born) son;
one born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather. *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 2.129.
A son born of a woman who has been previously married, whether she was previously intact or not, is a *paunarbhava*.
A son whom either the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* (given) son. *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 2.130.

One who is purchased by those two is "purchased" (krīta); one who is made so is "artificial" (kṛtrima), as is one who makes himself so. One who gives himself is "self-given" (svayamdatta); one conceived in the womb and born with the bride is "the son of a pregnant bride" (sahoḍhaja). Yājñavalkya 2.131.
But he who is taken up after having been abandoned becomes an *apaviddha* son;
among these, each subsequent one provides the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of the preceding.
This rule has been declared by me regarding sons born of wives of the same caste;
however, even one born to a Śūdra from a female slave through lust shall be a sharer of the inheritance.
Upon the death of the father, the brothers shall make him (the son of an appointed daughter) a recipient of half a share;
one who has no brothers shall take the whole, except for the sons of the daughters.
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, as well as their sons, the agnates, the kinsmen, the disciples, and those who have studied under the same teacher; Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.135.
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them is the heir to the wealth of the deceased;
for this rule applies to all castes in the case of one who has died without a son.
The heirs of forest-dwellers, renunciants, and lifelong students are, in order: the preceptor, the virtuous pupil, the spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred ford.
But a reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of one who was reunited, as well as of a uterine brother, whether that person be born or deceased. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.138)
But a uterine brother who is a reunited coparcener shall take the wealth, and not a non-uterine brother;
even one who is not reunited may take it, but a reunited brother born of a different mother shall not.
A eunuch, one who has fallen from caste, one born of such a union, a cripple, one who is insane,
one who is mentally dull, a blind person, and those afflicted by incurable diseases and the like, must be maintained by the family and shall receive no share of the inheritance.
However, their legitimate sons born of their own wives and those born of their wives through other men (kṣetraja) who are free from defects shall receive their shares;
and their daughters must be maintained until they are given away to husbands. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.141)
The childless wives among them who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
however, those who are unchaste as well as those who are hostile should be banished.

That which is given by her father, mother, husband, or brothers; that which is received in the presence of the nuptial fire; and that which is obtained upon supersession—these are proclaimed to be a woman’s property (*strīdhana*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.143)
Likewise, the property given by a kinsman, the nuptial fee, and the subsequent gift— these,
when she has died childless, her relatives shall obtain.
The property of a woman who dies without offspring belongs to her husband even in the case of the four [forms of marriage] beginning with the Brāhma;
however, if she has daughters, it belongs to them; in the remaining cases, it goes to the father.
Having given away his daughter, he who takes her back shall be punished and must pay the expenses along with interest;
if she has died, he may take back what was given after deducting the expenses incurred by both parties.
In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction,
a husband is not required to give to his wife the property he has acquired as her separate wealth.
One should give an equal amount as an "inducement for supersession" (ādhivedanika) to a wife who has been superseded;
however, if no separate property (strīdhana) was given to her, one should assign half of that amount. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.148)

When a partition has been concealed, the proof of partition should be known to arise from kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, documents, and separate holdings of houses and fields. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.149)

[9. Section on Disputes Concerning Boundaries] In a dispute over the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders, and others, the herdsmen, those who cultivate the borderlands, and all those who frequent the forests [shall decide]. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.150)
They should establish the boundary, marked by landmarks such as mounds, charcoal, husks, trees,
embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, and shrines.
Or the neighboring villagers from all four sides— whether four, eight, or even ten—
who are landholders, shall lead the boundary while wearing red garlands and garments.
But those who speak falsely shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement;
in the absence of witnesses or marks, the king is the establisher of the boundary.
This same rule is to be understood as applicable to groves, temples, villages, watering places, gardens, houses, and to rainwater, flowing streams, and the like.
In the case of breaking a boundary mark, as well as in the transgression of a limit,
and in the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middle, respectively.
However, a dam that causes little harm and brings about benefit is not to be prohibited;
nor is a well that takes water from another's land if it provides much water for one's own small field. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.156)
If one constructs an irrigation channel on a field without first informing the owner, the produce belongs to the owner;
in his absence, it belongs to the king. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.157)
If one neither cultivates a field that has been ploughed nor causes it to be cultivated, he shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation;
another person shall cause the field to be cultivated.

[10. Section on Disputes between Owner and Herdsman] A buffalo that causes damage to the crops shall be fined eight māṣas; a cow, half of that amount; and a goat or sheep, half of that again. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.159)
For those who sit down after having eaten [the fodder], the fine is double that which was stated;
for these same animals, even in a pasture, the fine for a donkey or a camel is equal to that for a buffalo.
As long as the crop is destroyed, the fruit shall belong to the owner of the field;
however, the cowherd is to be beaten, while the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.161)

There is no offense in [grazing] on a path, at the edge of a village pasture, or in a field, provided it is unintentional; but if it is done intentionally, one deserves punishment like that of a thief. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.162)

Large bulls, animals that have been set free, those born from a cow recently calved, newcomers, and others for whom there is no keeper— these are not to be claimed [as lost], even if they are overwhelmed by divine or royal calamities.
Just as a cowherd must return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening,
so too must one who has received wages be made to pay for those that have died or been lost through negligence.
But when damage occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, as well as the value of the property itself, for the owner.
The grazing of cattle may take place according to the desire of the villagers or by the authority of the king;
furthermore, a twice-born man may gather grass, firewood, and flowers from everywhere at all times.
The distance between fields within a village shall be one hundred bow-lengths;
for a market town (kharvaṭa) it shall be two hundred, and for a city (nagara) four hundred.
[11. The Section on Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner] One may recover one's own property sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the sale was not publicly declared.
He who buys from a low person in secret for a low price, or at an improper time, is a thief.
Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
and if there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize the person oneself and hand him over.

Purification comes from the appearance of the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the buyer recovers the price from whoever sold it to him. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.170)

A lost item must be recovered through legal testimony and by means of its enjoyment; otherwise, a fine of five times its value shall be imposed upon him, and if it is not recovered, that amount shall be paid to the king. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.171)
He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas.
If property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officials or local guardians, the owner may reclaim it within one year; after that period, the king shall take it.
One should pay one paṇa for a single-hoofed animal, four or five for a human, two each for a buffalo, a camel, or a cow, and one-quarter each for a goat or a sheep. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.174)

[12. Section on Non-delivery of Gifts] One's own property may be given without detriment to one's family, except for one's wife and sons; nor may one's entire estate be given when there are descendants, nor that which has been promised to another. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 2.175)
The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property;
and what has been promised as a gift must indeed be given, and once given, one must not take it back again.

[13. The Section on Regret Regarding Purchases] The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, jewels, women, milch cattle, and male slaves shall last for ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, or half a month, respectively. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.177)
Gold is not diminished when placed in fire; silver [loses] two palas per hundred;
tin and lead [lose] eight [palas per hundred]; copper [loses] five [palas per hundred]; and iron [loses] ten [palas per hundred]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.178)
In a hundred [palas] of wool, cotton, or silk thread, the increase is ten palas;
for medium quality, the increase is five palas, while for fine quality, it is considered to be three palas.
In woven cloth and in hair-cloth, a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized;
however, there is neither loss nor increase in silk and in garments made of bark.

Having ascertained the place, the time, and the nature of the enjoyment, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the goods lost, those who are experts shall declare what must be paid without doubt. Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.181.

[14. Section on Failure to Serve after Having Accepted Service] One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, or even one who has been sold, is released from that status by saving the life of his master, by abandoning his food, or by the payment of his ransom. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.182)
One who has been expelled from the order of renunciation becomes a slave to the king for life;
among the social classes, slavery is permitted only in the direct order of precedence and never in the inverse order.
Even when he has mastered the craft, the apprentice shall reside in the teacher's house for the prescribed period;
receiving his food from the teacher, he shall offer the fruits of his labor to him.

[15. The Section on the Breach of Agreements] Having established a residence in the city and appointed Brāhmaṇas there, the king should tell those learned in the three Vedas who receive a livelihood: "Let your own duty (svadharma) be protected. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.185)
But that which is established by convention, provided it does not conflict with one's own dharma, as well as any law enacted by the king, must also be protected with effort. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.186)
But he who misappropriates the property of the community, or whoever violates an agreement,
the king shall confiscate all his possessions and banish him from the realm.
The advice of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all;
whoever acts contrary to that should be made to pay the first fine. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.188)

The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the sake of the community's business with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business has been accomplished. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.189)
One who is dispatched for the business of a corporation shall deliver whatever he may obtain;
if he does not deliver it himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times that amount. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.190)
Those who know the Dharma, who are pure and free from greed, should be the ones who deliberate on affairs;
the word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.191)
This same rule applies to guilds, merchant corporations, heretical sects, and assemblies;
the king shall protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional way of life.
[16. Section on Non-payment of Wages] One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double;
if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount. The tools and implements must be protected by the servants. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 2.193.
But he who employs laborers without having fixed their wages must be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, or crops. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.194)
If one should disregard the place and the time, or should effect a profit in another manner, in that case it shall be at the pleasure of the owner; if more work has been done, more should be given.

Whatever amount of work one performs, for that much he shall receive his wages; if the task is impossible for both [master and servant] to accomplish, it is so; but if it is possible, one should perform it according to what was agreed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.196)
The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or fate;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.

If he abandons him on the way after he has set out, he must pay one-seventh of the fee; if he abandons him at the fourth stage of the journey, one-fourth; and if he abandons him halfway, he must pay the entire fee; the same applies to the one who causes him to be abandoned.

[17. Chapter on Gambling and Betting] When the stake involves interest of one hundred, the keeper of the gambling house shall take five percent from a rogue gambler, but ten percent from any other. *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 2.199.
Having been properly protected, he should give the king the share as it was determined;
he should cause the winner to take what was won, give it to the victor, speak the truth, and remain patient.

When the king has received his share and the assembly of gamblers is well-known, he shall cause the winner to pay the debt in a place where the court is present; otherwise, however, he shall not do so.

For they alone are the observers of legal proceedings and the witnesses; therefore, those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception should be banished by the king along with their stakes.
Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the purpose of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applying to betting on living creatures and to challenges to combat.

[18. Section on Verbal Abuse] If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, sensory organs, or afflicted by disease by means of praise that is true, false, or otherwise, he shall be fined twelve and a half *paṇas*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.204)
If a man swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king should compel him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.205)

The infliction of punishment should be carried out by considering the higher or lower status of the castes and classes: for offenses against those of lower dharma, the fine is half; for women of others and for those of superior rank, it is double.
In cases of defamation involving the reverse order of castes, the fines shall be double and triple;
for the direct order of castes, they shall be reduced by half and half again respectively.
In cases of verbal injury involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine shall be one *dama*;
for the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it shall be half of that. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.208)
But one who is unable and speaks thus should be fined ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is able should be made to provide a surety for his safety.
For an accusation made regarding an offense involving loss of caste (pātitya), the punishment is the middle amercement;
but for one associated with a minor offense (upapātaka), he shall be made to pay the first amercement.
For the expulsion of those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity, the fine is the highest amercement;
for castes and guilds, it is the middle amercement; and for villages and districts, it is the first amercement. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.211)

[19. Section on Physical Assault] But when a person has been killed without witnesses, the legal case must be investigated by means of physical marks, circumstantial reasoning, and oral testimony, for [an assailant] might create false marks out of fear. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.212)
A fine of ten paṇas is prescribed for touching ashes, mud, or dust;
double that amount is required for touching impure matter, the heel, or spittle.

The same [penalty] applies for women who are the wives of others; however, it is double for those of higher status, half for those of lower status, and there is no punishment when [the act is committed] through delusion, intoxication, and the like.
However, a limb that causes pain to a Brahmin may be cut off from one who is not a Brahmin;
if he merely raised his hand [to strike], the first amercement is the punishment, but for actual contact, it is half of that.
If hands or feet are raised [in a threatening manner], the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively;
but if all of them strike one another with a weapon, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, the fine shall be ten *paṇas*;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a cloth, or stepping on [the feet], the punishment is one hundred *paṇas*.
A man who causes pain with wood or other materials without shedding blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine shall be double.

For breaking or cutting off a hand, a foot, or a tooth, or for cutting off the ears or the nose, the middle amercement is the punishment; likewise for piercing a wound or for striking someone who is as good as dead.
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [senses];
or breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
For many who strike a single person, the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed;
for property taken during a quarrel, it must be restored, and the fine shall be double that amount.
But he who causes injury shall be made to pay the expenses arising from that undertaking,
as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel.
In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to fall,
one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of the damage.
One who throws into a house property that causes suffering or is life-threatening shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* as a fine for the first offense, and the middle amercement for the second.
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or cutting off a limb or member [of small animals],
the fine for small animals shall start from two paṇas and increase progressively.
For the cutting off of a male organ or for its death, the middle amercement shall be the fine;
for these same acts involving large animals, the punishment is double.
For cutting all the branches and trunks of trees that are capable of sprouting and growing,
and for cutting twenty trees that provide livelihood, the fine shall be double.
In the case of sacred monuments, cemeteries, boundaries, holy places, temples, and well-known trees, as well as for trees that have grown spontaneously, the fine is double. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.228)

For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines, the fine shall be half of that prescribed for the previously mentioned places. Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.229.
The Section on Violence] Violence (*sāhasa*) is defined as the forcible seizure of common property;
the fine for it is twice the value of that property, but if there is denial, it is fourfold. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.230)
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times the fine. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.231)

One who neglects the offering of water for guests (*arghya*), one who strikes his brother’s wife, one who fails to deliver a entrusted message, and one who breaks down a house situated by the sea; YDh_2.232.
For one who causes harm to neighbors, kinsmen, and others, the settled rule is that the fine for these shall be fifty paṇas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.233)
One who approaches a widow against her will, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help, one who cries out falsely, and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the highest castes; 2.234.

One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors, one who swears an improper oath, and one who performs the duties of an unfit person—[these are excluded]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.235)
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus; YDh 2.236.
A father, son, sister, brother, husband and wife, or teacher and pupil— whoever abandons any of these when they have not fallen from their caste— shall be liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
A laundryman who wears another's garment as his own shall be fined three *paṇas*;
however, for selling, hiring out, pledging, or borrowing it, he shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
In a dispute between father and son, the fine for witnesses is three paṇas;
for one who stands as an intermediary between them, the fine shall be eightfold.
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins,
as well as anyone who trades with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
He who declares a counterfeit coin to be genuine, or a genuine coin to be counterfeit—
that examiner of currency shall be made to pay the highest fine.

A physician who practices falsely shall be punished with the first amercement if the victim is an animal, the middle amercement if it is a human, and the highest amercement if the victim is a royal official. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.242)
He who binds one who should not be bound, he who releases one who has been bound,
and he who obstructs legal proceedings, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Whoever should take even an eighth part [of the value] by means of a scale or a balance, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this is ordained for both increase and decrease [in weight].
If one adulterates medicinal herbs, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses,
and other such commodities with inferior substances, he shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen paṇas.
For those who attribute a higher quality to clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark,
or cloth when they do not possess that quality, the fine shall be eight times the value of the saleable item.
For one who brings for deposit or sale a casket containing precious goods that is artificial,
a punishment shall be prescribed.
For breaking a vessel worth five *paṇas*, the fine is declared to be fifty; for one worth ten *paṇas*, it is one hundred;
for one worth twenty *paṇas*, the fine is two hundred; and as the price increases, the fine increases accordingly.
For artisans and craftsmen who, acting together, fix a price that causes distress,
or who knowingly cause a decrease or an increase in the price, the punishment is the highest amercement.
For merchants who, having come together, obstruct the sale of their merchandise by fixing an unreasonable price,
or who sell it [at such a price], the prescribed punishment is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
Whatever price is established for a commodity by the king, by that price its sale or purchase is conducted;
the surplus resulting from that is traditionally held to be the merchant's profit.
A merchant who buys and sells immediately may take five percent on goods produced in his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land.

Having deducted the expenses arising from the merchandise and placed them upon the value of the goods, a price that is beneficial should be established for both the buyer and the seller. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.253)

[21. Section on Non-delivery after Sale] He who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, shall be compelled to give it back with interest; or, if the buyer has come from a distance, he shall be made to pay the profit derived from that region. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.254)
Even if a sale has been completed, it may be rescinded if the previous buyer does not accept the goods;
for if the loss results from the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed belong to the buyer alone.
If a defect arises in the merchandise due to an act of the king or an act of God,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been requested, fails to deliver it.
If, having sold an item into the hand of another, one sells it again— whether it be defective or as if non-defective—
the fine in that case shall be double the price.

A merchant who, being unaware of the loss or increase of his merchandise, feels regret after having purchased it, shall not be permitted to rescind the sale; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth [of the value].
[22. Section on Joint Undertakings:

When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a collective association, the gain and loss shall be according to their respective contributions or as determined by their agreement. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.259)
If a deposit is lost through negligence—whether it was forbidden [to use] or not specifically entrusted—the owner shall pay for it;
furthermore, one who protects a deposit from loss is entitled to a tenth part of its value.
The king shall take a twentieth part as duty from the offering of *argha*;
however, that which is established by tradition (*vyāsiddha*), what is fit for the king, and what is sold [as such], shall go to the king. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.261)
One who speaks falsely regarding the quantity [of goods] while departing from the customs house,
as well as one who buys or sells with deceit, shall be made to pay eight times [the value].
A ferryman who collects a land toll shall be made to pay ten paṇas;
this same penalty applies for failing to invite Brāhmaṇas and neighboring residents.
When a deceased person has gone to another country, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives who have arrived there shall take his property; in their absence, the king shall take it.
They should abandon what is dishonest or profitless; one who is incapable should have the work performed by another.
By this, the rule for officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers has been declared.
[Chapter 23: On Theft] A thief is apprehended by pursuers either through stolen property or by his tracks;
likewise, one who has committed a prior offense and one who resides in an impure dwelling.
Others also should be suspected on account of their concealment of their caste, name, and so forth,
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and intoxicants, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered.
Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret;
those who have no income yet incur expenses; and those who sell goods that do not belong to them—[these are to be known as spies].
If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft does not clear himself,
he shall be made to restore the stolen property and be punished with the penalty prescribed for a thief.
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, the king should have him executed by various means of death;
however, having branded a Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him from his own kingdom.
If cattle are killed or stolen, the guilt falls upon the village headman if they have not yet left the village;
however, on the road, it falls upon the superintendent of the pasture, and outside the pasture, upon the one who apprehends the thief.
One should grant a village, or a plot of land where he travels,
or five villages outside the radius of one krośa, or even ten villages.
Those who capture bandits, those who steal horses and elephants,
and those who commit violent assaults, the king shall cause such men to be impaled upon stakes.
Those who commit the offenses of forcibly lifting [a garment] or breaking a sealed knot shall have one hand and one foot cut off;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of both hands and both feet.
For the theft of small, middling, or large property, the punishment shall be according to the value;
in the application of punishment, one must carefully consider the place, time, age, and capacity [of the offender].
If one knowingly provides a thief or a murderer with food, shelter, fire, water, mantras, or implements, he shall be subject to the highest fine.
For causing the miscarriage of a fetus by the discharge of a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed;
likewise for the killing of a man or a woman, either the highest or the lowest fine may be imposed.
Furthermore, having bound a stone to a woman who has committed adultery, who has killed her husband, who is not pregnant, or who has breached a dam, one should cause her to be immersed in water.
One who administers poison or sets fire [to a dwelling], or one who causes the death of her husband, her teacher, or her own child,
should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by cattle.
The sons and kinsmen of one who has been killed while unrecognizable must quickly investigate,
as must his wives who were devoted to other men, each separately.
Or, desiring [information about] women, wealth, or livelihood, he should ask people slowly: "With whom has this man departed? or "Is he near the place of death? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.281).
Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of a king, shall be burned by means of a straw fire.

[Chapter 24: On Adultery] A man shall be apprehended for adultery when he is caught by the hair with another's wife, or immediately upon the appearance of signs born of passion, or likewise when both parties confess it. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.283)
Grasping the knot of the lower garment, the breasts, the thighs, or the hair;
conversing in an improper place or time; and sitting together on the same seat. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.284)
In the case of forbidding [a man], a woman shall pay one hundred [paṇas] and a man two hundred;
but in the case of their actually preventing [the act], the punishment shall be the same as in the case of adultery (saṃgrahaṇa).
When the offender belongs to the same caste, the highest fine is prescribed; in the case of an act of intercourse with a woman of a lower caste, however, the middle fine applies.
In the case of intercourse with a woman of a higher caste, the man shall suffer death, while for the woman, the cutting off of the ears and other such punishments shall be inflicted.

For abducting a decorated maiden, the highest fine shall be imposed; otherwise, for women of the same caste, the lowest fine is prescribed; but in the case of abduction from a higher caste (prātilomya), death is ordained by law.
There is no offense if she consents and is of a compatible class; otherwise, there is punishment.
But for defilement, the hand shall be cut off; likewise, for a woman of the highest caste, there is death.
One should be made to pay one hundred in the case of defaming a woman, but two hundred for making a false accusation;
one approaching a lower-caste woman or a cow should be made to pay one hundred, and in the case of a woman of middle rank, the middle amercement.

A man who has intercourse with female slaves, female servants, or likewise with women kept by others— even if they are women with whom he is permitted to have relations— shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas.
For approaching a slave woman by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
if she is unwilling and he does so with many men, the fine for each is twenty-four paṇas.

A prostitute who has accepted her fee shall not, if she refuses to perform, be made to pay double; if the fee was not accepted, she should be made to pay an equal amount. A man likewise should be made to pay the same in such a case.
For one who has sexual intercourse with a woman in an improper place, or who urinates upon a man, the fine is twenty-four *paṇas*; the same applies for approaching a female ascetic.
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a male organ and banish him;
likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the lowest caste shall become an outcaste himself, while for a man of the highest caste approaching a woman of the lowest caste, the punishment is death.
[Chapter 25: Miscellaneous Matters] He who writes a royal edict deficient or excessive, or he who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.295)
One who defiles a twice-born man with forbidden food shall be punished with the highest amercement;
a Kṣatriya, with the middle amercement; a Vaiśya, with the first amercement; and a Śūdra, with half of that.
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall have three limbs maimed and be made to pay the highest fine.

The same fault incurred by using a four-legged animal applies to one who speaks thus: "Do not move away," as well as to one who uses wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, arms, or a pair of yokes. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.298)
If injury occurs by means of a vehicle with a broken nose-rope, or one with a broken yoke and so forth,
or if it retreats backward, the owner does not incur guilt.

Even if capable of doing so, a master who fails to rescue [his dependents] from fanged or horned animals shall pay the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, if they have cried out for help, he shall pay double.
One who falsely accuses a paramour of being a thief shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;
but one who releases him after having received wealth from him as a means of subsistence shall be made to pay that same amount multiplied eightfold.
One who speaks what is disagreeable to the king, one who reviles him, or one who divulges his secret counsel—having cut out their tongue, he should banish them. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.302)
The punishment for one who sells the body of a dead person, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the vehicle or the throne of a king, is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king,
and for a Śūdra living by the profession of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.
But having seen legal proceedings decided wrongly by the king,
the members of the court, together with the judge, shall be fined double the amount of the dispute.
If one who thinks "I am not defeated" is in fact defeated according to the rules,
he should be defeated again upon his return and made to pay double the fine.
The king, having reported to Varuṇa any unjust punishment he has inflicted,
should himself give to the Brahmins thirty times that amount as a fine.
[End of the Vyavahārādhyāya] [III. Prāyaścittādhyāya] [1. Āśaucaprakaraṇam]
One should bury a child less than two years of age and should not offer water for them thereafter;
others, however, followed by their relatives, should follow [the corpse] as far as the cremation ground.

If he has been initiated, he should be cremated with the worldly fire while those chanting the *Yamasūkta* and the *Gāthās* perform the rites according to the procedure for one who maintained the sacred fires, as if he were truly so.
On the seventh or even the tenth day, the kinsmen, facing the direction of the ancestors, enter the water with the mantra: "May the evil burn away from us. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.3)
In this same manner, the water-offering rite (udakakriyā) is performed for maternal grandfathers and teachers;
for friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests, the offering of water is optional.
Restraining their speech, they should pour water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage;
those who are students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) shall not perform this water-libation, nor shall those who are outcasts (patitas).

Heretics, those who have no protector, thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who go according to their lust, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide shall not receive the impurity rites nor the water libations. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.6)
When they have finished the water libations, emerged from the water, and are standing upon soft grass,
one should address those who have bathed with ancient historical narratives.
He who seeks a core in human existence—which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on the water—is utterly deluded. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.8)
If this body, which was composed of five elements,
has returned to its fivefold state through the actions arising from its own body, what cause is there for lamentation?
The earth, which carries all, goes to destruction; so do the oceans and the deities.
Since they are like foam, how will the world of mortals not go to destruction? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.10)

Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.11)
Having heard this, they should go home preceded by a child;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of their house.
Having sipped water and having touched fire and other elements, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds,
they should enter [the house], having anointed themselves and placing their feet slowly upon a stone.
For those who touch a corpse, even when performing rites such as entering [the village],
purification occurs instantly for them if they so desire, while for others it requires bathing and self-restraint.
Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or preceptor, one who observes a vow remains a vow-keeper;
he should not eat food from a person in distress, nor should he dwell with them.
Eating food that has been purchased or obtained, they should sleep separately on the ground;
for three days, food should be offered to the deceased according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña.
Water and milk should be kept for one day in an earthen vessel;
furthermore, the Vaitāna sacrifices, the domestic rites, and other ritual acts must be performed according to the injunctions of the Śruti.
Impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) is prescribed for three nights or ten nights;
however, in the case of a child under two years of age, the impurity of birth (sūtaka) belongs to both parents, yet it pertains to the mother alone.
Regarding the birth-impurity (sūtaka) of the parents, it certainly belongs to the mother because of the appearance of her blood;
on that day, [the father] is not defiled, because he was the cause of the previous [birth]. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.19)
In the interval between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days;
however, in the case of a miscarriage, nights equal in number to the months of gestation are the cause for purification.
In the case of those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for those who commit suicide, the impurity lasts for the duration of the period immediately following;
when that period is complete, one becomes pure after offering water libations.
For a Kṣatriya it is twelve days, for a Vaiśya fifteen;
for a Śūdra it is thirty days, or half of that for one who lives righteously.

For those who have not yet cut their teeth, impurity is said to last for one day; for those who have not yet received the tonsure ceremony, it lasts for one night; until the initiation into Vedic study (vratādeśa), it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, for ten nights.

But for [intercourse with] maidens who have not been given away, with children, and with the teacher’s pupil, a Vedic scholar, or a Śrotriya who is not a maternal uncle, purification is as follows. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.24)
In the case of sons other than those born of one’s own body, of wives who have gone to another man,
and when the king by whom one resides has died— that very day is the cause for purification.
A Brahmin should never follow after a Śūdra, nor a twice-born man ever follow after another. Having followed them, he becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
There is no period of impurity for kings, nor for those killed by lightning,
nor for one who dies in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, nor for one whom the king desires [to be pure].

Likewise for officiating priests and those initiated, while performing sacrificial rites; and for those observing the *sattra* vow, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.28)
In matters of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, or national upheaval, as well as in times of dire distress, immediate purification is prescribed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.29)

If he is touched by those who are menstruating or impure, he should bathe; if he is touched by them [in turn], he should sip water for purification. He should also mutter verses containing the word "water" and recite the Gāyatrī mantra once mentally.
Time, fire, ritual action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water, subsequent remorse, and fasting—all these are causes of purification. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.31)
For those who have committed improper acts, giving gifts effects purification; for a river, its current does so;
for that which is to be cleansed, earth and water do so; and for the twice-born, renunciation indeed effects purification. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.32)

Austerity is said to be the strength of those who know the Vedas, forbearance that of the wise, water that of the body, silent recitation that of those whose sins are concealed, and truth that of the mind. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.33)
For the elemental self (bhūtātman), austerity and knowledge are the means of purification; for the intellect (buddhi), it is wisdom (jñāna);
and for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), purification is considered supreme through the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.34)
[2. The Section on Duties in Times of Distress] In times of distress, a twice-born man may subsist by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even that of a Vaiśya;
having emerged from that distress and having purified himself, he should return to his own path. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.35)
Fruits, stones, linen, Soma, humans, cakes, creepers, sesame, boiled rice, meat broth, alkaline substances, curd, milk, ghee, and water. Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.36.
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, sacrificial grass, earth, leather, flowers, blankets made of goat hair, hair, buttermilk, poison, and soil; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.37.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, lead, Śakas, wet medicinal herbs, oil-cakes, and likewise animal perfumes; YDh 3.38.
Even when living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one should never sell sesame seeds;
for the sake of dharma, they may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
Lac, salt, and meat are causes for falling [from caste] if sold;
however, curd, milk, and liquor cause one to become of a lower varṇa.
A Brahmin who, when fallen into distress, accepts or eats food from anyone whatsoever, is not tainted by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.

Agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, trade by cart, mountain-mining, service to others, marsh-land cultivation, and the king—these, along with begging, are the means of livelihood in times of distress. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.42)
Having remained hungry for three days, one may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa;
having received it, it must be reported according to the law by the person who was approached.
Having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, study, austerity, and family, the king shall provide him with a righteous means of livelihood.
[3. Chapter on the Duties of the Forest-Dweller] Having entrusted his wife to his sons, or followed by her, the forest-dweller,
observing celibacy, shall go to the forest taking with him the sacred fire and the domestic hearth (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.45).

Self-controlled, wearing a beard, matted hair, and body hair, he should satisfy with food not grown by the plow the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.46)
One should accumulate wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been accumulated, one should relinquish it in the month of Āśvayuja.
Self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts,
devoted to Vedic study, habitually generous, and intent on the welfare of all beings.
Using his teeth as a mortar, eating only what is ripened by time, or using a stone for grinding,
he should perform his ritual actions and rites with the fruits and oils prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
One should pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, or always subsist on Kṛcchra penances; or one may eat once every fortnight, or once every month, or once every day has passed.

Being pure, he should sleep on the ground at night; during the day, he should pass the time by standing on tiptoe, or by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or likewise by the practice of yoga.

In summer he should stand amidst five fires, in the rainy season sleep on the bare ground, and in winter wear wet clothes; or else he should perform penance according to his ability. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.52)
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood—toward both of them alike, he is neither angry nor pleased. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.53)
Or, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, dwelling among trees and eating moderately,
he should beg for alms only for the sake of sustenance at the dwellings of forest-dwellers.
Or, having brought eight morsels from a village, he should eat them while restraining his speech;
or, subsisting on air, he should go toward the north-east until his body is withered away.

[4. The Section on the Duties of an Ascetic] Having performed from either the forest or the home the *prājāpatyā* sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (*sārvavedasadakṣiṇā*), and at its conclusion having consigned those fires into oneself; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.56.

Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, he should then set his mind on liberation; not otherwise. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.57)
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, tranquil, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot,
delighting in solitude, he should wander as a mendicant and resort to a village only for the sake of alms.
Free from greed, he should wander for alms at evening,
unobserved and in a secluded part of the village, seeking only enough to sustain his life.
The vessels of ascetics are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear toward living beings, the twice-born becomes immortal.
However, the purification of one's intention must be performed especially by a mendicant,
because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence.
One should contemplate dwelling in the womb, as well as the destinies born of karma,
mental anxieties, physical ailments, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of physical form.

Through the practice of meditation, one should perceive with subtle vision the self abiding within the self— the cycle of existence across thousands of births, characterized by the reversal of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
The stage of life is not the cause of dharma; rather, it becomes such when it is practiced [righteously].
Therefore, one should not do unto others that which is unwholesome for oneself. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.65)
Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, intelligence, fortitude, self-restraint,
control of the senses, and knowledge— all this is declared to be Dharma.
Just as sparks fly forth from a glowing mass of heated iron,
even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the Self.
In this regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some through its inherent nature, and some through habituation—consisting of dharma, adharma, or both. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.68)
The cause, the imperishable, the agent, the knower, the possessor of qualities, and the controller—though unborn, he is proclaimed "born" due to the assumption of a body. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.69)
Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, light, water, and earth—
each possessing one additional quality— so too does he take them up when coming into existence.
The sun is nourished by the oblation; from the sun comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen.
But when there is union between a woman and a man and the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord himself, as the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements.
The sense organs, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.73.
Effort, form, color, aversion to sound, existence, and non-existence—
all this is born of that beginningless one who desires a beginning.
In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, a congealing of the elements;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs.
From space [he obtains] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, strength, and so forth;
and from wind, the sense of touch, movement, expansion, and even dryness. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.76)
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, form, and luminosity;
from phlegm (rasa), however, come taste, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness. (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 3.77)
The unborn Self perceives the smell of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form; thereafter, it vibrates in the third month.
By not granting her longings during pregnancy, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman.
In the fourth month there is the stabilization of the limbs; in the fifth, the emergence of blood;
and in the sixth, the production of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair.
Endowed with mind and consciousness, and possessed of channels, sinews, and vessels,
he also possesses skin, flesh, and memory during the seventh and eighth months.
Furthermore, his vitality (ojas) flows away from the nurse, from the womb, and from himself;
thus, in the eighth month, the fetus born is deprived of life.
In the ninth or even the tenth month, he is expelled by the powerful winds of birth,
like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish pain.
His bodies are sixfold, and he possesses six layers of skin;
likewise, his limbs are six, and his bones number three hundred and sixty.
The teeth together with the sockets are sixty-four, the nails are twenty, and there are the long bones of the hands and feet; these constitute their four locations.
There are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the heels and four in the ankles;
there are four bones in the forearms, and exactly that many in the shanks. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.86)
One should designate two each as being produced at the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, the shoulder-blades, the armpits, and the pelvic bones. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.87)
There is one bone in the pubic region, forty-five in the back,
fifteen bones in the neck, one in each clavicle, and likewise one in the jaw.
At its base are two [bones]: the forehead-eye and the cheek; the nose consists of solid bone;
and the ribs, together with the sockets and the tubercles, number seventy-two.
Two temples, four skull-bones,
and likewise seventeen bones for the chest— this is the collection of bones in a person.
Smell, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ears are the sense organs.
One should know that the hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the feet are indeed the five organs of action; and the mind is of a dual nature.
The navel, the vital energy (*ojas*), the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples,
as well as the head, the shoulders, the throat, and the heart— these are the abodes of the life-force (*prāṇa*).
The omentum, the pericardium, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the two kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.94.
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the anus, the abdomen, and the two internal organs of the rectum—this is declared to be the extent [of the viscera]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.95)

The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-cavities, the two ear-flaps, the two ears, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two depressions of the loins; Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.96.
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, and the breasts are produced from the accumulation of phlegm;
likewise are the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the calves, thighs, and the muscles of the shanks.
The palm of the hand, the belly, the bladder-head, the chin, the two tonsils, and the nape of the neck—these are the locations on this body. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.98)
The two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the anus,
and the genitals— these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
There are exactly seven hundred veins, nine hundred sinews,
two hundred arteries, and five hundred muscles.
Know that there are twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred,
and fifty-six vessels known as sirās and dhamanīs.
It should be known that embodied beings have three hundred thousand hairs on their beard and head;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmans) and two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores,
sixty-seven hundred thousand, and an additional half [of a lakh] of hair-pores, along with the openings for sweat.
The atoms are reckoned as distinct by means of the winds; even though a single person may understand their nature and their arrangement. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.104)
Nine añjalis of chyle are to be known, ten of water;
seven indeed of feces, and eight of blood are proclaimed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.105)
Phlegm is six [parts], bile five, urine four, muscle fat three, and fat two; marrow is one, while the brain is above it. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.106)
"The bodily strength consists of phlegm, and the vital seed consists of that same [strength];
this body is thus unstable—he who strives for liberation is the one who should act. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.107)
Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā and Ahitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon.
The self situated in the center of that maṇḍala is like an immovable lamp;
it is to be known, and having known it here, one is not born again. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.109)
And that which I received from the Sun, the *Āraṇyaka*, as well as the Yoga-śāstra proclaimed by me, should be known by one who desires yoga. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.110)
Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses focused on no other object,
one should meditate upon that Lord who dwells as the Self within the heart like a lamp.
By reciting the Sāmaveda chant without error according to the prescribed rules,
one who is attentive attains the Supreme Brahman through that practice.
The Aparāntaka, Ullopya, Madraka, Prakarī, Auveṇaka, Sarobindu, and Uttara songs; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.113.

The *ṛc* verses, the *pāṇika* songs, those composed by Dakṣa, and the *brahmagītikās*—this is what is called "chanting" (*geya*); through the practice of this, it is designated as "liberation. (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 3.114)
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, is proficient in the musical scales and modes,
and understands the rhythm, attains the path of liberation without effort.
If one who knows music does not attain the supreme state through yoga,
he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.
The self is said to be beginningless, yet its beginning is the body;
the entire world originates from the self, and the self is born from the world.
How is it that this world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is deluded? And how did the Self arise within it? Tell us this. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.118)
Indeed, that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion is the thousandfold one,
possessing a thousand rays, a thousand eyes, and the splendor of the sun.
He is both the Self and the sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) whose form is the universe;
as Virāj, he attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food.
That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substance and deity,
having gratified the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit.
Then, having been joined with the wind, the Soma is led by the rays;
it is brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
From the orb of the sun, that sun emits the supreme nectar, which is the source of birth for all beings, whether they are of the nature of eaters or non-eaters. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.123)
From that food, again arises sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again ritual action.
Thus does this wheel, without beginning or end, revolve.
The self is beginningless; no origination exists for the inner self.
However, the person (puruṣa) is an inherent associate [of the body], born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.125)
The primordial deity whom I have described to you as the thousandfold self—
his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet became the social classes (varṇas) in their respective order.
From his feet the earth was born; from his head the sky arose;
from his nose the vital breaths; from his ear the quarters of space; from his touch the wind; and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun;
from his loins came the intermediate space and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings.
If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born in sinful wombs?
How is it that he, who is the Lord, is joined with undesirable states of being? (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.129)

Why is there no prior knowledge [of the soul] even though it is endowed with the instruments [of perception]? And why does the all-pervading [soul], though itself omnipresent, not experience the sensation [of others]? (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.130)
Through defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living being goes to the state of the lowest animals and plants, and wanders through hundreds of births and wombs.
And just as the bodies of embodied beings within their various forms are infinite,
so too are the forms of those possessing bodies here in all wombs.
The ripening of karmas for some occurs after death, while for others it arises in this very life;
for yet others it occurs both here and in the hereafter—such is the nature of things, and therein lies the purpose. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.133)
Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable, and being intent on what is false, one is born in other wombs. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.134)
A man who speaks falsehoods, as well as one who is slanderous, harsh,
or a speaker of idle gossip, is born among beasts and birds.
One who delights in taking what is not given, one who consorts with the wives of others,
and one who is violent toward immobile beings in an improper manner is born among stationary things.

One who knows the Self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses, performs dharma, and is learned in Vedic knowledge—such a person of sattvic nature attains birth among the gods. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.137)

He who delights in the doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause, who is undisciplined, enterprising, and a seeker of sense-objects— he, being of rajasic nature among men, attains birth after death.
One who is drowsy, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct, becomes a tamasic being among the animals.
Thus, pervaded by passion and darkness,
wandering here and joined with undesirable states, he enters the cycle of worldly existence.
For just as a dirty mirror is incapable of reflecting forms, so too an unripened faculty is incapable of self-knowledge. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.141)
Just as in an unripe mango, even though the sweet taste is present, it cannot be perceived;
so too, knowledge is not attained within oneself when the faculties are unripened. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.142)
An embodied being experiences all sensations within his own body, which is the substratum of them all;
but the yogi who is liberated does not experience any of these sensations.
Just as the single space appears distinct within jars and other vessels, so too the one Self appears manifold, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.144)
Brahman, ether, wind, fire, water, and earth are the constituent elements;
