these are the worlds, this is the Self, and from that [Self] comes all that is moving and unmoving. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.145)

within the womb by means of the qualities (guṇas). ||| Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.148 ||| Just as a single clay becomes a jar, a cup, a bowl, or other vessels according to the action performed, so the single Just as a goldsmith [fashions] a form by taking mere gold as his material, or as a silkworm produces a cocoon through the union with its own saliva; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.147 //
Having thus taken up these causes, the Self, having come together with the instruments, creates itself within those various wombs here.
The great elements are real, and the self is likewise;
for who, having seen with one eye, sees again with the other? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.149)
Who indeed understands speech once it has been heard again and again?
To whom belongs the memory of past objects, and who is the creator of dreams? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.150)
Proud on account of birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth, he exerts himself toward objects such as sound through action, mind, and speech. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.151)
With a mind full of doubt as to whether the fruit of action exists or not, he is deluded; for even though he is unaccomplished, he considers himself accomplished. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.152)
"My wife, my sons, and my ministers—I am theirs": such is his state;
he always possesses a perverted mind regarding things that are beneficial or harmful. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.153)

One who makes no distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower, or between primordial nature and its transformation, and who exerts himself in fasting, entering fire, or leaping into water; YDh 3.154.
One who behaves in this manner, being undisciplined in self and possessed of false attachments, is bound by action through hatred, delusion, and desire. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.155)

Service to the teacher, discernment regarding the meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures, the performance of those duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.156)
Abstaining from looking at or touching women, beholding the Self within all beings,
renouncing possessions, and wearing worn-out saffron robes.
Restraining the senses from their objects, abandoning drowsiness and laziness,
reflecting upon the nature of the body, and perceiving evil in worldly activities.

Through these means— purity of the *sattva* quality by being free from *rajas* and *tamas*, freedom from longing, and tranquility— one who is thoroughly purified becomes fit for *sattva* and attains immortality.
Through the application of mindfulness to reality, through the practice of yoga, through the exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, the union with the Truth proceeds.
He whose mind, established in *sattva* and focused on the Lord, remains unshaken at the dissolution of the body, shall attain the full recollection of his former births. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.161)
Just as Bharata colors his own body with various pigments, creating diverse forms, so too does the Self [assume] bodies born of karma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.162)

The deformity of the fetus at birth, such as being deficient in limbs and so forth, is seen to result from defects in time, karma, the self, the seed, and likewise from those of the mother. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.163)
This self has never at any time been liberated from egoism, the mind, the sense of motion, the fruit of karma, and the body. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.164)
Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the vessel, and the oil, so too is its alteration observed; likewise, the premature exhaustion of the vital breaths occurs.
Infinite are his rays, like those of a lamp situated in the heart;
they are white, black, variegated in form, tawny, blue, and red.
One among them stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [path] one goes to the supreme goal. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.167)
That other hundred rays of his which are established upwards,
by means of them he reaches the bodies of the gods together with their abodes.
Those multiform rays of his that are below possess a mild radiance;
by means of them, he wanders helplessly in this world for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his karma.
By means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge; by birth and death;
by affliction, departure, and likewise arrival; and indeed by truth and falsehood. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.170)
[One should not be concerned] with superior states, with pleasure and pain, with auspicious and inauspicious actions,
or with the results arising from the knowledge of omens, birds, and the conjunctions of planets.
By the movements of the stars and constellations, by waking states as well as those born of dreams, and likewise by space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness; YDh 3.172.
Through the Manvantaras, through the attainment of the Yugas, and even by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, and fruits,
one perceives the Self as wealth, as well as the cause of the world.

Egoity, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude, the transition between the various senses, desire, retention, and life—these [are the functions of the mind]. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.174)
Heaven, dreaming, the impulse of entities, the movement of the mind, the winking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and the grasping of the five elements [are his work]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.175)
Since these marks of the Supreme Self are perceived,
therefore there exists a Self beyond the body, the all-pervading Lord.

The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action, as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the elements beginning with earth; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.177.
The unmanifest Self is declared to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this field;
it is the Lord dwelling within all beings, which is both being and non-being, and that which is both existent and non-existent.
The arising of the intellect (buddhi) is from the unmanifest (avyakta); from that, the emergence of the ego (ahaṃkāra);
and from the ego, the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the rest, each possessing one additional quality [in succession].
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever among these has emerged from which [element], that dissolves back into that very same one. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.180)
I have explained to you how the Self creates itself, even though it is the Lord, through the ripening of the three kinds of karma. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.181)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are proclaimed to be its very qualities;
indeed, when possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel.
He alone is the supreme Puruṣa, both without beginning and yet possessing a beginning;
he is declared to be subject to transformation, having a form perceivable by the subtle body and the senses.

Between the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) and the path of the stars (ajavīthī), and between [the regions] of Agastya—by that way those who maintain the sacred fire and desire heaven proceed toward the celestial realm. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.184)
And those who are devoted to generosity and endowed with the eight qualities correctly,
they too, being dedicated to the vow of truth, follow that very same path.
Among them, eighty-eight thousand sages were householders;
they were subject to rebirth, yet they served as seeds and propagators of the Dharma.
Between the Seven Sages and the Nāgavīthī, there dwell those who have taken refuge in the world of the gods;
they are likewise sages, entirely free from all worldly undertakings.
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings.
For from it [the Veda] proceed the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the sciences,
the Upaniṣads, as well as the verses, the aphorisms, the commentaries, and whatever else constitutes the realm of speech.
The recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint,
faith, fasting, and independence are the causes for the knowledge of the Self.
For he is indeed to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
furthermore, he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard from by the twice-born.
Those twice-born who, having resorted to the forest, find Him thus and worship the Truth with supreme faith— Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.192.
In due order, they proceed to the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice,
the world of the gods, the sun, and the lightning.
Then a person born of the mind approaches them and leads them to the world of Brahman;
for them, there is no return to this world again.
For those men who have won heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts, [the path] consists of smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.195)
The world of the ancestors, the moon, the wind, rain, water, and the earth—in this sequence they arise here, and they return there once again. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.196)
The self-possessed man who does not understand these two paths shall become either a venomous serpent, a moth, an insect, or a worm. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.197)
With the feet placed upward on the thighs, having laid the right hand upon the left, slightly raising the face and steadying it with the chest; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.198.
With eyes closed, established in sattva, not touching the teeth with the teeth, the tongue resting motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly steady; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.199.
Having restrained the collection of the senses, and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) twice or even thrice.
Then the wise man, maintaining concentration (*dhāraṇā*), should hold his self there, meditating upon that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 3.201.
Invisibility, memory, luster, vision, as well as the power of hearing, and the ability to enter another's body after casting off one's own. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.202)
The power to create objects at will is indeed the mark of perfection in yoga;
when yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body is fit for immortality.
Alternatively, even by reciting the Veda while dwelling in the forest, having renounced ritual actions,
eating only what is unasked for and being moderate in diet, one may attain supreme perfection.
For even a householder who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests,
who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth, is indeed liberated.

[5. The Section on Expiation] Having experienced the terrible and dreadful hells born of mortal sins (mahāpātaka), those who have committed such great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.206)
The slayer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a deer, a horse, a pig, or a camel; the drinker of spirituous liquor enters the womb of a donkey, a Pulkasa, or a Śvapāka—of this there is no doubt.
A stealer of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a moth;
and one who violates the Guru’s bed shall gradually become a blade of grass, a shrub, or a creeper.

The killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; the drinker of spirituous liquor shall have black teeth; the stealer of gold shall have deformed nails; and the violator of the Guru’s bed shall suffer from skin disease.
Whosoever lives among these [sinners] is born with their characteristic mark:
a stealer of food shall be afflicted with disease, and a stealer of speech shall be mute. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.210)
One who steals grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a foul-smelling nose;
one who steals oil, the habit of drinking oil; and a backbiter, a foul-smelling mouth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.211)
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest.
One who steals the jewels of others will be born into a low caste;
by killing a peacock, one becomes a leaf-eating bird; and by stealing fragrant substances, one becomes a muskrat.

A mouse shall be the stealer of grain; a camel the vehicle; a monkey the fruit; a water-fowl the water; a crow the milk; and a house-builder (the white ant) the household utensils. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.214)

A honey-thief becomes a gadfly; a thief of meat, a vulture; a cow-thief, a monitor lizard; likewise, a fire-thief, a crane; a thief of cloth, one with white leprosy; a thief of liquids, a dog; and a stealer of salt, a cricket.
This has been stated by me merely as an illustration regarding the act of theft;
for just as there are various kinds of objects, so too are there various classes of living beings.
Having obtained the fruit according to their karma, through the passage of time they are born as animals;
then, having fallen from auspicious marks, they become impoverished and the lowest of men.
Then, having become free from stain, they are born into a great family as enjoyers of life,
endowed with knowledge and possessed of wealth and grain.
Through the non-performance of what is enjoined, through the practice of what is censured, and through the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.219)
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become pleased with him. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.220)
Men who do not perform expiation for their sins, being devoted to evil deeds and devoid of remorse, go to terrible and dreadful hells. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.221)
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.222)
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃprapātana,
the great hell Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Mahāpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, likewise Asipatravana, and Tāpana— the twenty-first.
Worst among men, burdened by the terrible sins arising from the great transgressions as well as those arising from the minor transgressions, go [to hell] without having performed expiation.
Sin committed through ignorance is removed by expiatory rites;
however, one who acts out of desire becomes fit for social intercourse here only by virtue of a scriptural declaration.

The killer of a Brāhmaṇa, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed—these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is he who lives in association with them. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.227)
Excessive reviling of gurus, disparagement of the Vedas, the killing of a friend, and the loss of what has been studied should be known as equal to the murder of a Brahmin. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.228)

Eating what is forbidden, deceitfulness, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.229)
The seizure of a horse-jewel, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow,
as well as the misappropriation of a deposit, is indeed equal to the theft of gold.

Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage, and daughters-in-law is recorded in tradition as equal to violating the Guru’s bed.
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, the daughter-in-law, the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter; YDh 3.232.
But he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed;
having had his penis cut off, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing.
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling goods unfit for sale, and gambling; YDh 3.234.
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, a younger brother marrying before his elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.235.
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censured wealth;
atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.
The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice;
the abandonment of one's father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.237)

Defiling a maiden, officiating at a sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother, giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, crookedness, and the violation of a vow; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.238.

Engaging in undertakings for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning the study of the Vedas, the sacred fires, and one's sons, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.239.

Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, harming women, living by the sale of medicinal herbs, the construction of murderous machines, vices, and the selling of oneself—these are [grounds for loss of caste]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.240)
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
Studying false scriptures, claiming authority regarding the sources [of knowledge],
and the sale of one's wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).
Carrying a skull as his bowl, bearing a banner, subsisting on alms, and making his deed known,
the slayer of a Brahmin shall attain purification after twelve years by eating sparingly.
One may attain purification by rescuing a Brāhmaṇa, or by saving twelve cows,
or likewise by performing the purificatory bath at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice.
Having seen on the road a Brahmin or even a cow afflicted by a long-lasting or severe disease, the slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure by restoring them to health.

Having been brought before [the court], if his entire property has been confiscated, or if he has been killed, or if he has been wounded by weapons for that reason, he is purified even while still alive. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.246)
Saying "Svāhā to the body hairs," he should indeed offer his body, beginning with the hair and ending with the marrow, with these mantras in the proper sequence. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.247)
Or, being made a target and slain in battle, he attains purification;
even if still alive but rendered as good as dead and afflicted by wounds, he is purified. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.248)

Having recited the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times in the forest while remaining self-controlled, he shall be purified; or he may be purified by eating sparingly while traveling upstream along the Sarasvatī.
Or, by giving sufficient wealth into the vessel, one may attain purification;
for the sake of the purifier's own purification as well, the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice is prescribed by tradition.
One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall observe the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, one who destroys an embryo or kills an Ātreyī woman shall observe the same vow according to the respective caste.

One should observe the vow even if one does not kill, provided one has come together for the purpose of killing; however, if a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a sacrifice is killed, one should prescribe a double vow.
Having drunk any one of liquor, water, ghee, cow’s urine, or milk that has been heated until it resembles fire,
the drinker of liquor attains purification through death.
Either clothed in hair or wearing matted locks, he shall perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin;
or he shall eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for three years.
But having drunk liquor, or [consumed] semen, feces, or urine through ignorance,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again.
That Brahmin woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of the ancestors;
even in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, or a sow.
A Brahmin who has stolen gold, however, shall offer a mace to the king;
having confessed his deed, he is purified whether he is killed by it or even if he is released. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.257)
Having informed the king, one who performs the vow for the drinker of spirituous liquor shall be purified;
or he may give gold equal to his own weight, or give what brings satisfaction to a Brahmin.
He shall lie upon a heated iron bed together with an iron woman;
having had his testicles cut off and seized, he shall cast away his body in the direction of Nirṛti.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for three years,
or he may practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance while reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā for three months.
He who indeed lives with these for a year becomes equal to them;
he may marry a maiden from among them who is fasting and possesses nothing.
Having killed all those who have fallen from their caste,
even a Śūdra, though devoid of [Vedic] entitlement, becomes purified by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for this duration of time.

The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for a month, remaining self-controlled, sleeping in a cow-pen, and following after cows; he becomes purified by the gift of a cow.
Or, being composed, he should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and one bull as a gift.
Purification for a minor offense (upapātaka) may be achieved in this manner by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
or by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance.
For killing a Kṣatriya, a man should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh,
or he may perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years.
The killer of a Vaiśya shall perform this penance for one year or give one hundred cows;
the killer of a Śūdra shall perform it for six months, or else give ten milch-cows.
Having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly,
one should give, respectively, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep for the sake of purification.
Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra;
likewise, for killing a thousand vertebrate animals, or a cartload of invertebrate animals.
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
For an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and sheep, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull].

Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous animal, a peacock that frequents water or land, or a vulture, one should give a cow; however, for killing a non-carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
For killing snakes, an iron rod [should be given]; for a eunuch, tin and lead;
for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; and for a horse, a fine cloth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.273)

But one who is unable to give the gift of a drona of sesame seeds for each of the [animals] beginning with the elephant, such as the partridge, shall perform a Kṛcchra penance for the purification of each individual.
Upon killing a living being produced from fruit, flowers, food, or sap, one should consume clarified butter;
for killing something with bones, something small should be given as a gift; but for a boneless creature, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc* verses should be recited;
for the useless cutting of medicinal herbs, one should subsist on milk and follow cows for a day.
One bitten by a harlot, a monkey, a donkey, a camel, or the like, or by a crow,
becomes pure by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) in water and consuming clarified butter.
With the two verses beginning "That semen of mine today," one should consecrate the spilled semen;
with that [semen], one should touch the space between the breasts and the middle of the eyebrows using the ring finger.
Seeing one's own reflection in water, one should mutter "May splendor be in me";
and when one has seen something impure, or when there is fickleness, or even when speaking untruth, one should mutter the Sāvitrī.
A student of sacred knowledge who, while observing celibacy, approaches a woman becomes an *avakīrṇin*;
he is purified by sacrificing an ass as an animal offering to Nirṛti.
But having neglected the alms-gathering and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill,
he should offer two oblations with the two [verses] beginning "kāmāvakīrṇaḥ."
Then one should perform the ritual attendance with the mantra "saṃ mā siñcantu";
however, for eating honey or meat, a *kṛcchra* penance must be performed, as well as the remaining vows.
Having acted contrary to the teacher's will, one is purified only by propitiating him;
if the teacher is sent on a mission and dies, the pupil shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
But there is no sin if a Brahmin dies while assistance is being rendered;
nor is there sin when bulls are in the process of digestion, or during the administration of medicine or fire-rites.
The fault of one who makes a false accusation is twice as great as that of one who speaks the truth;
furthermore, by speaking falsely, he incurs the very fault of the person he has falsely accused. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.284)
He who falsely accuses another of a great sin or a minor sin should subsist on water for one month, reciting prayers with his senses restrained.
One who has been falsely accused should perform a difficult penance, or specifically the Āgneya penance;
he should offer a Puroḍāśa cake to Agni, or even an animal sacrifice to Vāyu.
One who approaches his brother’s wife without being authorized should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having approached a woman in her courses, he becomes pure by consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights.
One who performs sacrifices for those unworthy of them (vrātyas), even if performing malevolent rites, shall perform three kṛcchra penances;
likewise one who has forgotten the Veda, one who eats barley for a year, and one who has abandoned one who has sought refuge. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.288)
Dwelling in a cow-pen for one month as a celibate student, subsisting on a diet of milk and devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, he is purified from the acceptance of gifts from the wicked.

One who performs breath control (prāṇāyāma), one who has bathed in water after riding a donkey-cart or a camel, one who has bathed naked, and one who has eaten or had sexual intercourse with a woman during the day—[must perform penance]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.290)
Having addressed a guru with "huṃ" or "you," or having defeated a Brahmin in debate, or having bound him with a garment, one must quickly appease him and fast for a day. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.291)
If one raises a staff against another, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if one strikes him down, it is an *atikṛcchra*;
if blood flows, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and if there is internal bleeding, it is a *kṛcchra*.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin,
an expiation should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been stated.
His own relatives should have a slave-girl carry a pot [filled with impure matter] outside the village;
they should exclude the outcast from all social dealings.
When he has returned having fulfilled his vow, they should pour out a new jar [of water] for him;
they should not despise him, nor should they live with him in any way whatsoever.
This same rule is proclaimed for women who have fallen from their status:
they should be given a dwelling at the edge of the house, along with food, clothing, and protection.
Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming one's husband—these also are certainly specific causes of downfall for women. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.297)

One should not live together with those who harm those who have sought refuge, children, or women—even if they are otherwise observant of their vows—nor with these who are ungrateful. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.298)
When the funeral vessel has been set aside, he who stands among his kinsmen should first offer fodder to the cows;
for this is the true honoring of one who has already been honored by the cows.
One whose fault is publicly known should perform a vow approved by an assembly;
however, one whose fault is not publicly known should practice a secret vow. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.300) [Secret Expiation]
Having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while submerged in water, even a killer of a Brāhmaṇa is purified by giving a milch cow.
Saying "Svāhā to the body hairs," he should then subsist on air for a day, or,
standing in water, he should offer forty oblations of clarified butter.

Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, a pure man who has stolen the gold of a Brāhmaṇa becomes purified by reciting the Rudra hymns while standing in water.
One who recites the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn] is liberated from the sin of violating the Guru’s bed;
at the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow must be given separately by each of these [offenders].
One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins,
indeed for those arising from minor offenses (upapātaka) and for that which is specifically unenjoined.
Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink purifying Soma water consecrated with the syllable *oṃ*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.306)
Whatever may have been done out of ignorance, whether by night or by day,
all that perishes through the performance of the twilight devotions at the three times of the day.
The recitation of the Śukriya and the Āraṇyaka, and especially that of the Gāyatrī, as well as the Rudraikādaśinī, are indeed removers of all sins. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.308)
And wherever a twice-born man considers himself defiled,
there he should perform an oblation with sesame seeds and likewise recite the Gāyatrī mantra.

Sins, even those arising from the great crimes (mahāpātaka), do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and who is intent on the performance of the five sacrifices. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.310)
Subsisting on air, standing during the day and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun,
one is purified from all sins except the killing of a Brahmin by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times.
Celibacy, compassion, patience, generosity, truthfulness, sincerity,
non-violence, refraining from theft, sweetness, and self-control— these are remembered as the *yamas*.

Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.313)
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, one should fast on the following day; thus one performs the *Sāntapana Kṛcchra*.
When one observes a six-day period with each of the various *sāntapana* substances followed by a day of fasting,
this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana* penance.
When one drinks, respectively and daily, water infused with leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, lotus, and *bilva* trees, along with *kuśa* grass, it is declared to be the *parṇakṛcchra* penance.
One should drink hot milk, ghee, and water, each for one day respectively, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for,
and by fasting, this is proclaimed as the Pādakṛcchra penance.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold rite is called the Prājāpatya;
this very same rite becomes an Atikṛcchra when one eats only as much food as fills the palm of the hand.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days;
the *parāka* is proclaimed to consist of fasting for twelve days.
The daily consumption of oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, and barley meal, followed by a fast for one night, is called the *saumya-kṛcchra*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.321)
Through the practice of each of these for three nights in succession,
this is to be known as the "tulāpuruṣa" penance lasting fifteen days.

While performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should take rice-balls the size of a peacock’s egg, increasing them according to the lunar days during the bright fortnight, and decreasing them by one each day during the dark fortnight. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.323)
Alternatively, one may subsist for a month on exactly two hundred and forty morsels of food; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.324)
One who bathes at the three sessions of the day should perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
he should mutter purificatory mantras and consecrate the morsels of food with the Gāyatrī.
Purification for unspecified sins is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.326)
One who performs the Kṛcchra penance with a desire for dharma shall attain great prosperity;
being well-concentrated, he obtains the fruit of a major sacrifice.
Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya, the ṛṣis spoke thus to that high-souled lord of yogins of immeasurable splendor: [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.328]
Those who, unwearied, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and thereafter go to the third heaven.
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; likewise, one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
one desiring long life shall obtain long life; and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity.
For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a *śrāddha* ceremony, there shall be inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.331)

By the retention of this scripture, a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of being a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.332)
If a learned man causes this to be heard by the twice-born on every festival day, may you grant your approval that he shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.333)
Having heard this speech of the sages, Yājñavalkya, with a joyful heart,
said, "So be it," after bowing down to the Self-Existent One.
